mainText: The timing of your last meal of the day can play a vital role in helping your body function optimally. Here are five health benefits of having an early dinner. Having an early dinner helps optimise digestion and metabolism. It helps maintain the body's circadian rhythm, which improves sleep quality. Eating late in the night can negatively impact your blood pressure. An early meal helps maintain healthy blood pressure and reduces the risks of heart attacks. Eating early helps maintain proper insulin levels, which is beneficial for regulating blood sugar levels. An early dinner helps reduce the risk of gastrointestinal diseases and burning sensations. It helps prevent bloating and provides relief from acid reflux. An early dinner helps burn fat, improves metabolism, and curbs cravings, aiding in weight loss.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Biden hosts star-studded NYC fundraiser with Obama and Clinton - BBC.com
mainText: US President Joe Biden hosted a record-breaking election fundraiser in New York City, alongside his predecessors Barack Obama and Bill Clinton. The star-studded evening at Radio City Music Hall was expected to raise over $25m for the campaign, setting a new record for a single political event. The fundraiser aimed to extend the growing cash gap between President Biden and his Republican challenger Donald Trump, as polls suggest the race for the White House is on a knife edge. The event was attended by a crowd of 5,000 Democrats, including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, who urged attendees to do whatever they could to ensure that the 'dishonest, chaotic, ineffective regime of Donald Trump' did not return. The event was hosted by comedian Mindy Kaling and featured performances by stars such as Queen Latifah and Cynthia Erivo. However, the highlight of the evening was the appearance of the three presidents - Biden, Obama, and Clinton - which was met with chants of 'four more years' for Biden. The discussion between the three presidents was moderated by comedian Stephen Colbert. During the discussion, Biden reiterated that democracy was at stake in this election, criticizing Trump's support of those who participated in the 6 January Capitol Riot and his endorsement of authoritarian leaders abroad. Obama praised Biden's legislative victories, while Clinton accused Trump of claiming overnight successes that were actually the result of Obama's administration. The event ended with the four men donning aviator sunglasses in an impression of Biden, earning a standing ovation from the audience.

author: HT News Desk
title: Mukhtar Ansari news LIVE: Mortal remains being brought to Ghazipur - Hindustan Times
mainText: Gangster-turned-politician Mukhtar Ansari died of cardiac arrest at a hospital in Uttar Pradesh's Banda on Thursday. Ansari was brought to the Rani Durgavati Medical College from the district jail in an unconscious state after he had complained of vomiting. Despite the efforts of a team of nine doctors, Ansari succumbed to cardiac arrest. Preparations for the funeral of the gangster-turned-politician are underway at the Kali Bagh Graveyard in Ghazipur. Security has been tightened across Uttar Pradesh, and the family alleges 'slow poisoning' in jail. Two days before his death, Ansari was admitted to the same medical college when he complained of abdominal pain and was unable to pass stool for four consecutive days. He was discharged after 14 hours and sent back to Banda jail. Ansari's family members had earlier expressed apprehension that he could be killed in a fake encounter. On March 13, Ansari was sentenced to life imprisonment in a case related to the use of forged documents for obtaining an arms licence in 1990.

author: Elizabeth Robinson
title: Illinois stabbing survivors describe attack and Evan Gershkovich detained for a year: Morning Rundown - NBC News
mainText: An Illinois mother, Darlene Weber, credits her son and their dog with saving her life during a stabbing spree that left four people dead. The attacker, a 22-year-old man, went on a rampage, killing four people and injuring seven others, including Weber and her two children. Weber described the attacker as looking like 'the devil incarnate' and said that if it wasn’t for her son, she might not have survived. During the attack, Weber was stabbed in the face by the man. As she crawled through the house screaming for her son to help her, their dog bit the man, giving Weber enough time to escape. When Weber’s son, Jacob Vollman, confronted the attacker, the man charged at him. Despite the attacker turning his attention to Weber’s daughter, Cathy Gilfillan, Vollman was able to keep fighting him off. Gilfillan said that if it wasn’t for Vollman, she and her mother would not be here. The suspect, Christian Soto, was arrested on charges of murder, attempted murder, and home invasion. Soto’s attorney said he admitted to the crimes and that he had taken marijuana he believed was 'laced with an unknown narcotic', causing him to become paranoid. Among those killed are Jay Larson, a mail carrier who was on the job when he was attacked, and 15-year-old Jenna Newcomb, who died saving her sister, officials said.

author: Amy Cassidy, Sarah Dean
title: South Africa bus crash kills 45 people - CNN
mainText: A tragic incident occurred in South Africa's Limpopo province on Thursday when a bus carrying worshippers to an Easter festival plunged off a bridge and burst into flames, killing at least 45 people. The country's transport department confirmed the death toll and reported that one person is seriously injured. The sole survivor of the crash is an eight-year-old child who has been airlifted to a hospital for medical attention. The passengers were pilgrims traveling from Gaborone, the capital city of the neighboring country Botswana, to a church for an Easter conference. The crash took place in the Mamatlakala mountain pass between Mokopane and Marken. After falling, the bus reportedly caught fire. The cause of the crash is currently under investigation. According to reports, the driver lost control and the bus fell onto a rocky surface, some 50 meters under the bridge, and caught fire. Efforts are ongoing to recover the bodies of the passengers who were killed. Some bodies burned beyond recognition, while others are trapped inside the debris or scattered on the scene. South African Transport Minister Sindisiwe Chikunga expressed her condolences to the families affected by the tragic bus crash and urged responsible driving at all times, especially during the Easter weekend when more people are on the roads.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Virat Kohli Stares At Gautam Gambhir Ahead Of Mega IPL Clash. KKR Posts Photo That 'Hit Hard' - NDTV Sports
mainText: Ahead of a major Indian Premier League (IPL) clash, a photo of Virat Kohli staring at Gautam Gambhir has been posted by Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR), which has made quite an impact. The photo, which shows Kohli in an intense stare-down with Gambhir, has been described as 'hitting hard'. The two cricketers, who have had their share of on-field confrontations in the past, are set to face each other in a high-stakes IPL match. The photo has added to the anticipation and excitement surrounding the match. Both Kohli and Gambhir are known for their aggressive approach to the game, and their face-off is expected to be one of the highlights of the match. The photo has been widely shared on social media, with fans eagerly awaiting the clash between the two cricketing giants.

author: Lee Moran
title: Seth Meyers Bursts Trump Supporters' Bubble With 1 Line From Truth Social Filing - HuffPost
mainText: Seth Meyers, the host of 'Late Night', has burst the bubble of Trump supporters with a single line from the Truth Social filing. Meyers pointed out that the stock value of Trump's newly Nasdaq-traded Trump Media & Technology Group, which is currently soaring, is based entirely on Trump's brand. He argued that Trump supporters are artificially propping up the value of the company, the central product of which is the Truth Social platform that Trump uses for his regular rants. Meyers also noted that in its own SEC filings, the company admitted that Trump could tank the value of the company if he is found guilty amid his myriad legal woes. The organization, which is making losses, is an 'abject failure' with dwindling users, according to Meyers. He described it as just 'a dumb Twitter ripoff for MAGA trolls'. Meyers stated that Trump's stock market windfall has nothing to do with the reality of his business and that it is obvious to everyone. He said that it is just a buying spree fueled by Trump supporters and traders capitalizing on the enthusiasm of Trump supporters.

author: HT News Desk
title: Rahul Gandhi's big Lok Sabha poll promise for women - Hindustan Times
mainText: Congress MP Rahul Gandhi has made a significant promise for the upcoming Lok Sabha elections. He has pledged that if his party comes to power, they will reserve 50 per cent of government jobs for women. He questioned why the representation of women in the system is so low when the population of women in India is 50 per cent and their presence in higher secondary and higher education is also 50 per cent. He stated that the Congress party wants 'Aadhi Abaadi Poora Haq', meaning that they understand that women's potential will be fully utilised only when women have equal contribution in the government running the country. The Congress party has decided that half the recruitment for all new government jobs should be reserved for women. They are also in favour of the immediate implementation of women's reservation in Parliament and in assemblies. Gandhi added that women with a secure income, future, stability and self-respect will truly become the strength of society. He said that having women in 50 per cent of government posts will give strength to every woman in the country and powerful women will change the destiny of India.

author: Bernd Buchmasser
title: Drake Maye details pro day meeting with Patriots - Pats Pulpit
mainText: Drake Maye, the North Carolina quarterback, has detailed his pro day meeting with the New England Patriots. Maye is considered one of the top quarterback prospects in the 2024 NFL Draft and has been linked with the Patriots, who are in need of a quarterback. During his pro day, Maye showcased his arm strength, accuracy, and mobility, all of which have made him a highly sought-after prospect. He also had a meeting with the Patriots, which he described as 'productive'. The Patriots' representatives were reportedly impressed with Maye's performance and his understanding of the game. Maye stated that he had a good conversation with the Patriots and felt that he was able to show them his capabilities. The Patriots have been actively scouting quarterbacks ahead of the draft, and Maye is among the players they are considering. The team's decision will likely depend on how the first round of the draft unfolds. If Maye is still available when the Patriots are on the clock, there is a possibility that they could select him.

author: Science Desk
title: Japan’s SLIM moon lander survives another lunar night against all odds - The Indian Express
mainText: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) confirmed on Thursday that its SLIM Moon lander survived two lunar nights without its instruments freezing. The Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, launched in September last year, landed on the Moon on January 19. Despite landing in a less-than-favourable position, it was able to do something that ISRO’s Chandrayaan-3 could not — not once but twice. SLIM’s landing made Japan just the fifth country in the world to soft-land a spacecraft on the Moon after the United States, the Soviet Union, China and India. However, the 200 kilogram lander actually landed on its nose that day and it went dark shortly after since it was not in a great position for its solar panels to harvest sunlight. But it came back to life again on January 28, and it went on to gather science data. Shortly after that, JAXA teams put the lander in hibernation mood ahead of its first lunar winter. SLIM had already succeeded with its main mission objectives — demonstrate a soft-landing, collect science data and deploy two small rovers. And it was expected that its instruments would not survive the harsh lunar night when temperatures can be below minus hundred degrees Celsius. But it survived the lunar night not once but twice, according to a JAXA post on X, formerly Twitter. “According to the acquired data, some temperature sensors and unused battery cells are starting to malfunction, but the majority of functions that survived the first lunar night was maintained even after the second lunar night,” said a post shared by the agency on the platform.

author: Paul Myerberg
title: Terrence Shannon powers Illinois to Elite Eight amid controversy - USA TODAY
mainText: Terrence Shannon Jr., the senior star of the Illinois basketball team, led his team to the Elite Eight of the NCAA men's tournament, despite picking up his fourth foul with 11:17 left in the East Region semifinal. At that point, Illinois was leading Iowa State 51-42. When Shannon returned to the game with 5:38 left, the lead had been cut to 55-51. However, Shannon quickly made his presence felt, scoring a 3-pointer to extend the lead to 59-54. He scored another six points in the final stretch of the game, including a slam dunk that made the score 70-64 with 24 seconds left. Illinois eventually won the game 72-69. Shannon scored 29 points in the game, along with five rebounds, three steals, and two assists. Despite his impressive performance, Shannon is a polarizing figure. He was suspended by the university in December after being arrested and charged with rape. The suspension was reversed after six games by a federal judge who ruled that Illinois had violated Shannon's civil rights. Shannon has not spoken to the media during the tournament on the advice of his legal counsel.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Salman Khan reflects on his bond with late actor Satish Kaushik: 'He was also there in...' - The Times of India
mainText: Bollywood superstar Salman Khan recently attended the Mumbai screening of 'Patna Shuklla.' He came to support his brother Arbaaz Khan, who is the producer of the film. The movie features notable actors such as Raveena Tandon, Satish Kaushik, and Anushka Kaushik, among others. During interaction with the media, Salman became emotional while reminiscing about Satish Kaushik. Expressing his sentiments, Salman remarked, 'Satish ji humare bade hi close the… The most amazing thing is that he completed each of his projects he took on before his death. He was also there in 'Kisi Ka Bhai Kisi Ki Jaan.' The late actor portrayed a judge's role in 'Patna Shuklla.' Satish had shared a group photo with Salman and Arbaaz upon completing 'Patna Shuklla' in December 2022. Veteran actor, director, and producer Satish Kaushik passed away on March 9 last year.

author: Michelle Ye Hee Lee, Min Joo Kim
title: Russia veto brings end to U.N. panel monitoring North Korea sanctions - The Washington Post
mainText: On Thursday, Russia vetoed a U.N. resolution, effectively ending the monitoring of U.N. sanctions against North Korea over its nuclear program by United Nations experts. The sanctions themselves, however, remain in place. The veto came during a vote on a U.N. Security Council resolution that would have extended the mandate of a panel of experts monitoring sanctions on North Korea for a year. But due to Russia's veto, the panel's operation will now halt when its current mandate expires at the end of April. This move sparked Western accusations that Moscow was acting to shield its weapons purchases from North Korea for use in its war against Ukraine, in violation of sanctions. Russia's U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia told the council before the vote that Western nations are trying to 'strangle' North Korea and that sanctions have proven 'irrelevant' and 'detached from reality' in reining in the country's nuclear program. U.S. Deputy Ambassador Robert Wood accused Russia of attempting to silence the panel’s 'independent objective investigations' because it 'began reporting in the last year on Russia’s blatant violations of the U.N. Security Council resolutions'.

author: Chantal Da Silva, The Associated Press
title: Israeli court halts subsidies for ultra-Orthodox who don't serve in army - NBC News
mainText: The Supreme Court of Israel has ordered an end to state funding for ultra-Orthodox yeshiva students who do not serve in the army. This ruling could potentially destabilize the leadership of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as he navigates conflicts with Hamas in Gaza and disagreements with key ally the United States. The Israeli government has until Monday to present a new military conscription plan. This comes amidst public anger over exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox from military service, a longstanding point of contention that could now lead to political upheaval. The court's decision puts additional pressure on Netanyahu, whose fragile governing coalition relies in part on two ultra-Orthodox parties that have insisted on maintaining the exemptions. If Netanyahu's government collapses, Israel would be forced into new elections, which polls suggest Netanyahu would likely lose. The Supreme Court also issued an interim order blocking the government from funding monthly subsidies for yeshiva students who are between the ages of 18 and 26 and have not received a deferral from the military in the past year. The funds are to be frozen starting April 1. This ruling will affect about a third of the roughly 180,000 seminary students who receive subsidies from the government for full-time studies.

author: Saurav Mukherjee
title: Afghanistan news: Taliban to recommence stoning for women accused of adultery, says report | Mint - Mint
mainText: The Taliban's Supreme Leader Mullah Hibatullah Akhundzada has announced that women in Afghanistan will be stoned to death for adultery. This announcement was made in a voice message on state TV last Saturday. Akhundzada stated that the international community had been advocating for women's rights, which were against the Taliban's interpretation of Islamic Sharia. This move has been met with horror by Afghan women's rights groups, who say that the dismantling of any remaining rights and protection for the country's women is now almost complete. They argue that the Taliban's announcement has been enabled by the international community's silence. The Taliban's work did not end with the takeover of Kabul, it has only just begun.

author: saumya pandey
title: Linking Synaptic Proteins To Autism: Understanding The Molecular Blueprint | TheHealthSite.com - TheHealthSite
mainText: The article discusses the critical role of gene regulation in shaping synaptic architecture. Groundbreaking research conducted by Kobe University scientists has provided invaluable insights into the molecular mechanisms governing synaptic development and its implications for neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Synapses, the connections between brain cells, undergo dynamic changes during development, yet the molecular mechanisms behind these changes remain largely unknown. This knowledge gap hinders progress in understanding and treating neuropsychological disorders like ASD. These findings not only advance our knowledge of synaptic biology but also hold significant promise for the development of targeted interventions and therapies for individuals affected by neurodevelopmental disorders. By elucidating the molecular underpinnings of synaptic development and dysfunction, researchers are poised to make strides toward more effective treatments and improved outcomes for individuals with ASD and related conditions. The article also discusses the concept of synaptic pruning, the process of reducing connections between brain cells after early childhood. However, the molecular processes driving synaptic changes remain elusive, posing challenges for disorder treatment. The research approach involves analyzing synaptic proteins using advancements in proteomic analysis and marmosets as model organisms. The researchers led by TAKUMI Toru delve into synaptic protein dynamics to shed light on synaptic development. Their study, published in Nature Communications, unveils temporal changes in synaptic protein expression post-birth, driven by gene regulation. Mice and marmosets exhibit distinct timings in protein regulation, suggesting evolutionary brain differences. Recognizing ASD's association with synaptic developmental anomalies, researchers probe protein-level alterations. They find gene expression patterns in ASD patients align with synaptic protein changes seen during prenatal and neonatal periods. Insights into synaptic protein dynamics offer potential avenues for disorder treatment development. Understanding molecular mechanisms behind synaptic development is crucial for addressing neuropsychiatric disorders like ASD and schizophrenia. The research provides essential proteomic datasets for further exploration of synaptic development and inter-species disparities.

author: MD Ijaj Khan
title: 5 things about AI you may have missed today: AI tool DrugGPT helping doctors, AI solutions for cybercrime and more - HT Tech
mainText: This article highlights five key developments in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) that you might have missed. First, an AI tool called DrugGPT is helping doctors prescribe medicines safely in England. The tool, developed by Oxford University, provides instant second opinions by analyzing patient conditions, suggesting drugs, and highlighting potential adverse effects. Second, Shikha Goel, Additional DGP and director of TS Cyber Security Bureau, has urged technology professionals to develop AI solutions for combating cybercrime. She spoke at the AI Days 2024 conference, emphasizing the transformative power of AI in law enforcement and the need for innovative AI tools to analyze data, predict crime, and enhance communication for police forces. Third, Intel's latest Core Ultra processors, which feature built-in neural processing units (NPU), are targeting content creators and gamers. These chips promise faster performance and native AI capabilities. Fourth, the BJP plans to use an AI-driven real-time translation tool, Bhashini, embedded in the Namo app, to overcome language barriers in southern India. Lastly, the article discusses the potential misuse of AI by criminals and the need for safeguards.

author: Anadolu Agency
title: Health experts advocate digital health tech for cancer care revolution | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
mainText: Health experts are emphasizing the importance of digital health technologies in revolutionizing cancer care. These technologies have the potential to significantly improve patient outcomes, enhance early detection, and streamline treatment processes. In recent years, digital health tools have gained prominence in various aspects of healthcare. From telemedicine platforms to wearable devices, these innovations offer new ways to monitor patients, provide personalized interventions, and collect real-time data. For cancer care, digital solutions can play a crucial role. Here are some key areas where digital health technology can make a difference: 1. Early Detection: Digital tools can aid in identifying cancer at earlier stages, leading to more effective treatment options and improved survival rates. 2. Remote Monitoring: Patients can be monitored remotely using wearable devices and mobile apps, allowing healthcare providers to track symptoms, medication adherence, and overall well-being. 3. Personalized Treatment Plans: Digital health platforms enable personalized treatment plans based on individual patient data, genetic profiles, and treatment responses. 4. Data Analytics: Advanced analytics can process large datasets to identify patterns, predict outcomes, and optimize treatment strategies. 5. Patient Education and Support: Digital resources provide educational materials, support groups, and information to empower patients and their families. However, challenges remain, including data privacy concerns, interoperability issues, and ensuring equitable access to digital health solutions. As the field continues to evolve, collaboration between healthcare professionals, technology developers, and policymakers will be essential to harness the full potential of digital health in cancer care.

author: Piyali Bhadra
title: Home remedies to improve vitamin B12 deficiency in the body - The Times of India
mainText: A deficiency in vitamin B12 can lead to weak muscles, trouble walking, fatigue, and an increase in the heart rate. It also leads to premature aging with wrinkles and loose facial skin. Here are some dietary home remedies that would help in improving vitamin B12 deficiency in the body. Milk and dairy products are good sources of vitamin B12, one cup of whole milk consumption with curd or ghee consumed once a day would help you increase the level of vitamin B12 in your body. For vegetarians, consumption of cereal is a good source of vitamin B12 in the body. Though, they are synthetically made regulated portions every day can help increase the vitamin level. Yeast is filled with minerals and vitamins. Fortified yeast which is grown in food but not as a leavening agent contains quite a good amount of vitamin B12. Consumption of 15 gms every day is more than enough. People who have issues consuming milk products can opt for non-dairy milk such as almond, soy, or rice milk which are fortified. Fish is one of the rich sources of protein and omega-3 fatty acids, it is also a good source of vitamin B12. Mainly consumption of shellfish and salmon fish would help you increase B-12 in the body. Vitamin B12 is found in around 46% of eggs. Therefore, the consumption of two eggs every day is a good source of vitamin B12 for your body and they also get absorbed by the body easily and quickly. The consumption of chicken or goat meat is a good source of B12 and also is rich in protein, iron, and zinc which keeps the body glowing and healthy. Chicken liver is packed with nutrients and is considered one of the richest sources of vitamin B12.

author: Neha Yadav
title: 6 hydrating vegetables to have in summers for weight loss - Hindustan Times
mainText: In the summer, eating foods that are rich in water content can help detoxify your body, keep you hydrated, and promote weight loss. Here are some hydrating vegetables you can eat in the summer to support weight loss. Cucumbers, which have a high water content, help hydrate your body. They are low in calories and perfect for your diet in the summer to lose weight. Celery is a hydrating leafy vegetable with a high water and fiber content. It is excellent for your weight loss diet as it helps satisfy hunger and eliminate excess fat. Lettuce is a water-rich cruciferous vegetable that helps aid weight loss and digestion. This vegetable is rich in fiber, which helps reduce hunger pangs. Asparagus is an ideal vegetable for your weight loss diet as it is full of fiber and water content. Brussels sprouts are low in calories and high in fiber. They are hydrating vegetables that help detoxify your body, provide essential nutrients, increase metabolism, and help reduce weight. Carrots are excellent water-rich vegetables that are low in calories. They have carotenoid antioxidants that help prevent weight gain and increase satiety.

author: Lifestyle Desk
title: Is social anxiety holding you back? Recognise the signs to cope with it - The Indian Express
mainText: Social anxiety is a disorder that can create significant obstacles in a person's life. It can obstruct their capacity to meet and interact with others, leading to increasing isolation and overwhelming feelings of loneliness. Unlike shyness, which can affect daily interactions with others to some extent, social anxiety can be life-altering as it prevents the person from doing even the most mundane tasks such as shopping or taking a walk outside. Dr Rahul Chandhok, head psychiatrist and head consultant, Mental Health and Behavioural Science, Artemis Hospitals, describes it as a pervasive and often debilitating psychological condition where an individual experiences an extreme fear of being a part of social situations and interactions. He adds that the symptoms can be felt physically, emotionally, and behaviourally. Physical symptoms include experiencing rapid heartbeat, sweating, trembling, nausea, and difficulty breathing. Emotionally, people with social anxiety are likely to feel extreme self-consciousness, dread, or panic in social settings. Behaviourally, such people may avoid social situations altogether or endure them with extreme discomfort. Dr Vijayshree Bajaj, psychologist and mental wellbeing coach at MedyMind adds that if left untreated, this form of anxiety can significantly impact an individual's daily life, relationships, and overall well-being. Genetics, environmental factors, parenting style, social media, and early social development are some of the factors that contribute to social anxiety. The symptoms of social anxiety majorly impact a person's quality of life, resulting in missing out on important social, academic, or professional opportunities and contributing to feelings of loneliness, isolation, and low self-esteem.

author: Pravrajya Suruchi
title: 8 easy ways to increase immunity - DNA India
mainText: Boosting immunity is crucial for maintaining good health. Here are eight simple ways to enhance your immunity. Prioritize Sleep: Strive for 7-8 hours of quality sleep each night. During sleep, your body releases cytokines, proteins that aid in combating infections. Manage Stress: Persistent stress can weaken your immune response. Implement relaxation techniques to manage stress effectively. Eat a Balanced Diet: Consuming a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains provides your body with the necessary vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants for optimal functioning. Stay Hydrated: Water plays a vital role in numerous bodily functions, including the immune system response. Aim to drink eight glasses of water daily. Exercise Regularly: Engaging in moderate exercise aids your body in eliminating bacteria and can enhance immune function. Consider Probiotics: Probiotics are beneficial bacteria that can improve gut health, which may indirectly support your immune system. Wash Your Hands Frequently: This simple yet effective practice can prevent the spread of germs and reduce your risk of infection. Limit Added Sugar and Processed Foods: Excessive intake of sugar can suppress immune cell function. This information is not the opinion of DNA but is obtained from media reports.

author: Pravrajya Suruchi
title: Soaked dry fruits to have on an empty stomach - DNA India
mainText: The article discusses the benefits of consuming soaked dry fruits on an empty stomach. It mentions that soaking almonds for a few hours can soften their texture and potentially make them easier to digest. Similarly, soaking figs can make them plumper and potentially enhance their natural sweetness. Raisins, when soaked for a short time, may become plumper and easier to chew. They offer a good source of iron, and some potassium. Dates, when soaked, can soften their texture and make them easier to digest. They are a good source of natural sugars, fiber, and potassium. Soaking prunes can significantly soften their texture and potentially aid digestion due to their high fiber content. Soaked apricots can add a pleasant sweetness and some vitamins like A and C to your breakfast. Soaking cashews can improve their creamy texture and potentially make them easier to digest. The article concludes by stating that these soaked dry fruits can be a healthy addition to your breakfast routine.

author: Lifestyle Desk
title: This is how your circadian rhythm affects kidney health - The Indian Express
mainText: The article explains the relationship between your sleep-wake cycle, also known as your circadian rhythm, and your kidney health. Dr H.S Bhandari, a nephrology and dialysis specialist at Ujala Cygnus Group of Hospitals, highlights that while you're sleeping, your kidneys are actively working. Adequate sleep is essential for the body's repair and regeneration process, which includes your kidneys. Disruptions in sleep or irregular sleep patterns can interfere with this vital repair function, potentially damaging your kidney health. The article also points out that the impact is bidirectional. If you have existing kidney problems, particularly chronic kidney disease, your sleep can be affected. Conditions like nocturia (excessive urination at night) or restless legs syndrome can disrupt your sleep. The hormone melatonin, which regulates sleep, may also play a role in kidney function. The article provides tips for maintaining a kidney-friendly sleep cycle, such as prioritizing a regular sleep schedule, practicing good sleep hygiene, embracing a healthy lifestyle, managing stress, and seeking professional help if you have pre-existing kidney conditions or sleep disorders. By prioritizing a healthy sleep routine and maintaining a healthy lifestyle, you can promote both restful nights and optimal kidney function.

author: TN Health Desk
title: Deadly Strep Throat Infection Surges In Japan: Know Symptoms And Preventive Measures - Times Now
mainText: The article reports a surge in potentially deadly strep throat infections in Japan. The Japanese health authorities have issued a warning about the increase in infections, with cases in Tokyo being about three times higher than in 2023. Nationwide, diagnoses of streptococcus bacteria of the throat are being made at four times the rate of the past five years. As of March 10, Japan recorded 474 cases of the more serious streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (SSTS), which has a fatality rate of up to 30%. This syndrome occurs when the infection spreads throughout the body, potentially causing organ failure. The disease is not a respiratory illness like pneumonia or Covid-19, so it is unlikely to lead to a pandemic situation. Dr Hitoshi Honda, an infectious disease professor at Fujita Health University, stated that this is a droplet infection and emphasized the importance of hand hygiene in preventing invasive streptococcal infections. The surge in cases reportedly led the North Korean soccer team to abruptly cancel a World Cup qualifier match in Japan last week.

author: Shriya Raina
title: Sunscreen: Physical vs Chemical Sunscreens - The Times of India
mainText: The article provides a comprehensive comparison between physical and chemical sunscreens. Physical sunscreens work by creating a barrier on the skin's surface that reflects and scatters UV rays away from the skin. They contain mineral components such as titanium dioxide and zinc oxide, making them suitable for sensitive skin types. They offer broad-spectrum protection against both UVA and UVB rays and start working immediately after application. On the other hand, chemical sunscreens absorb UV rays and convert them into heat, which is then released from the skin. They contain organic compounds such as octinoxate, oxybenzone, and avobenzone. Despite their lightweight and non-greasy texture, which makes them easier to apply and suitable for daily use under skincare or makeup products, they may not be suitable for people with sensitive skin due to the potential for irritation and allergies. The choice between physical and chemical sunscreens depends on individual skin type, preferences, and sun exposure. The article emphasizes the importance of understanding the differences between these two types of sunscreens to make an informed choice.

author: Doric Sam
title: United States residents are becoming more and more susceptible to a hard-to-spot illness: 'That could be playing a role here' - The Cool Down
mainText: The article reports on the increasing susceptibility of United States residents to Lyme disease, a hard-to-spot illness. As temperatures continue to rise, the risk of Lyme disease is increasing, with a recent surge in confirmed cases causing concern among experts. The Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention reported a record 2,904 Lyme disease cases in the state in 2023, a significant increase from 2,617 in the previous year. Lyme disease is primarily transmitted to humans through bites from deer ticks. One of the factors contributing to the rise in cases is the increase in ticks in the nymph stage, which are more difficult to detect and can be more lethal when it comes to spreading tick-borne illnesses. Deer ticks are expanding their range farther north and east, a trend attributed to climate change, which is enabling ticks to take advantage of warmer temperatures. The number of ticks in the nymph stage submitted for testing doubled last year. The small size of these ticks often leads to them going undetected on the body, increasing the likelihood of them staying attached longer than usual. This difficulty in detection could be playing a role in the increase in Lyme disease cases. Lyme disease can cause symptoms ranging from fatigue, headaches, and skin rashes to more severe symptoms such as joint, heart, and nervous system damage. Early detection and treatment with antibiotics can effectively manage the disease, but the common symptoms make the disease difficult to spot. The article includes the story of a woman who suffered debilitating headaches and swelling in her knee that eventually left her unable to walk without crutches. She was initially recommended physical therapy, but her symptoms worsened. After getting checked out at an orthopedic clinic, her knee was drained and tested, and she was diagnosed with Lyme disease. She made a full recovery after receiving rounds of IV antibiotic treatment in the hospital and at home. The article concludes by noting that Maine is not alone in facing the increased risk of Lyme disease, with areas in central and eastern Canada, which were not previously prime tick territory, slowly becoming hotspots for these disease-carrying critters.

author: Youri Benadjaoud
title: Mpox is on the rise: Who's eligible for a vaccine, and do you need a booster? - ABC News
mainText: The article reports on the increasing cases of Mpox, formerly known as Monkeypox, in the United States. The number of infections has nearly doubled compared to the same time last year, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The majority of the reported cases are either unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals. The Jynneos vaccine, which comes in two doses, is recommended for those who have been exposed to someone with Mpox or those who had a sex partner in the past 2 weeks who was infected. Currently, there are no recommendations for a booster. The vaccine is also recommended for those who identify as gay, bisexual, or a man who has sex with other men who have had more than one sexual partner or been diagnosed with more than one sexually transmitted disease in the past six months. Those with immune-compromising conditions, such as HIV, are also eligible. Locations offering the free vaccine can be found on the CDC website. The article emphasizes the importance of these preventive measures in the public health response to curb the increase in Mpox cases. The Mpox virus does not discriminate and will spread between any two people. The vaccine primarily works to protect against severe illness, though it may not guarantee avoiding infection. It typically takes about two weeks after the second dose to reach full protection. Vaccines don't always 100% prevent disease, they ultimately reduce the severity of disease. Therefore, seeing people contract Mpox after vaccination is not unexpected. However, less severe disease has been observed in the majority of patients with Mpox in this current outbreak.

author: VOA Learning English
title: Scientists Say Bird Flu Is Hurting World’s Seal Population - VOA Learning English
mainText: The article reports on the impact of the bird flu outbreak on the world's seal population. The bird flu outbreak, which began in 2020, has led to the deaths of millions of domesticated birds and has also affected wildlife populations. The virus is not currently considered a threat to humans, but experts warn that its continued spread could increase risks to humans. The bird flu has killed tens of thousands of seals and sea lions in various parts of the world, causing significant economic losses at poultry farms and harming wild birds. Seals and sea lions in areas such as Maine in the northeastern United States and Chile in South America have been affected. The virus has been identified in seals on both the eastern and western coasts of the United States, with at least 300 seals dying from bird flu in New England and somewhat smaller numbers dying in Washington state's Puget Sound. The situation is also severe in South America, where more than 20,000 sea lions have died in Chile and Peru, and thousands of elephant seals have died in Argentina. The virus can be controlled in domesticated animals, but it can spread quickly among wildlife and ocean mammals. For example, in South America, seals that have never been infected with the virus have suffered huge losses. Once the virus is in wildlife, it spreads rapidly as long as there are susceptible animals and species. The movement of animals spreads the virus to new areas. Scientists are still researching how the seals got infected, but it is most likely from contact with infected seabirds. The death rates have been high in South America since bird flu arrived late in 2022, with hundreds of thousands of birds in Peru and Chile dying from the virus since then. The worldwide outbreak is continuing, and the virus was even found for the first time in mainland Antarctica in February. Scientists have said bird flu might also have played a part in the deaths of hundreds of endangered Caspian seals in Russia last year. The deaths of seals and sea lions can hurt environments where the sea creatures are near the top of the food chain. Seals help keep the ocean in balance by preventing overpopulation of the fish they feed on.

author: The Conversation
title: Lots of People Die Every Year During or After Sex. An Expert Explains Why. - ScienceAlert
mainText: Sex is a common activity, but it can sometimes have serious consequences. Every year, people die during or after sex, and the reasons behind these fatalities can be complex. In an article published in The Conversation, Dr. Tania Gergel, a research associate at King’s College London, delves into the factors that contribute to these deaths. One significant cause is cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes. During sexual activity, the heart rate and blood pressure increase, which can strain the cardiovascular system. For individuals with pre-existing heart conditions, this added stress can be dangerous. Additionally, certain medications, like Viagra, can further elevate the risk of cardiovascular events during sex. Sudden arrhythmia death syndrome (SADS) is another factor. This condition involves irregular heart rhythms that can lead to sudden cardiac arrest. Although rare, it can occur during sexual activity. Autoerotic fatalities are tragic incidents where individuals accidentally cause their own deaths while engaging in self-stimulation. These cases often involve asphyxiation or other risky behaviors. Positional asphyxia is a risk when certain sexual positions restrict airflow. In some cases, individuals may inadvertently block their own airway, leading to suffocation. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a type of stroke that can occur during sex due to the sudden increase in blood pressure. It can lead to severe headaches, loss of consciousness, and even death. Dr. Gergel emphasizes the importance of recognizing these risks and seeking medical advice if you have underlying health conditions. Communication with sexual partners about any health concerns is crucial, and understanding warning signs during sex can help prevent serious incidents. While sex is a natural and enjoyable part of life, being informed about potential risks ensures a safer experience for everyone.

author: India Education Diary Bureau Admin
title: New research by a team of MIT engineers offers a guide for fine-tuning specific material properties. - India Education Diary
mainText: A team of engineers from MIT has conducted new research that provides a guide for fine-tuning specific material properties. This research is particularly relevant when it comes to materials properties at the micro- and nano-scales. Scientists have known for decades that while bulk materials behave in certain ways, those rules can break down for materials at these scales, often in surprising ways. One such surprise was the discovery that applying even modest strains on materials can dramatically improve certain properties, as long as those strains stay elastic and do not relax away by plasticity, fracture, or phase transformations. Micro- and nano-scale materials are especially good at holding applied strains in the elastic form. The MIT researchers have developed the first-ever map of how to tune crystalline materials to produce specific thermal and electronic properties using a combination of first principles calculations and machine learning. The team, led by Ju Li, the Battelle Energy Alliance Professor in Nuclear Engineering and professor of materials science and engineering, described a framework for understanding precisely how changing the elastic strains on a material can fine-tune properties like thermal and electrical conductivity. The work is described in an open-access paper published in PNAS. 'For the first time, by using machine learning, we've been able to delineate the complete six-dimensional boundary of ideal strength, which is the upper limit to elastic strain engineering, and create a map for these electronic and phononic properties,' Li says. 'We can now use this approach to explore many other materials. Traditionally, people create new materials by changing the chemistry.'

author: India Education Diary Bureau Admin
title: Persistent “hiccups” in a far-off galaxy draw astronomers to new black hole behavior - India Education Diary
mainText: A supermassive black hole at the core of a distant galaxy appears to be experiencing what can best be described as 'hiccups'. This unusual behavior, never before observed in black holes, has been discovered by astronomers from MIT, Italy, the Czech Republic, and other places. The black hole, which was previously silent and is located at the center of a galaxy approximately 800 million light-years away, has suddenly become active, emitting gas plumes every 8.5 days before returning to its usual quiet state. The scientists believe that these periodic outbursts are most likely caused by a second, smaller black hole that is orbiting the central, supermassive black hole and ejecting material from the larger black hole's gas disk every 8.5 days. The team's findings, which are published today in the journal Science Advances, challenge the traditional understanding of black hole accretion disks, which were thought to be relatively uniform gas disks rotating around a central black hole. The new findings suggest that accretion disks may contain a more diverse range of contents, possibly including other black holes and even entire stars. 'We thought we knew a lot about black holes, but this is telling us there are a lot more things they can do,' says study author Dheeraj “DJ” Pasham, a research scientist in MIT’s Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research. 'We think there will be many more systems like this, and we just need to take more data to find them.' The study's MIT co-authors include postdoc Peter Kosec, graduate student Megan Masterson, Associate Professor Erin Kara, Principal Research Scientist Ronald Remillard, and former research scientist Michael Fausnaugh, along with collaborators from multiple institutions, including the Tor Vergata University of Rome, the Astronomical Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences, and Masaryk University in the Czech Republic.

author: Jamie Carter
title: Space photo of the week: James Webb telescope reveals surprising starburst in ancient galaxy - Livescience.com
mainText: The James Webb Space Telescope has captured a new image of the irregular dwarf galaxy I Zwicky 18, located 59 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major. This image, published on March 26, 2024, reveals that the galaxy has experienced several sudden bursts of star formation. The European Space Agency (ESA) explains that the galaxy's low content of heavy elements, those heavier than hydrogen and helium, makes it typical of the galaxies that existed in the early universe. The galaxy's core features two distinct bright areas filled with stars, with the youngest stars believed to be in the northwest region. These areas are surrounded by brown filaments, which are gas bubbles heated by stellar winds and intense ultraviolet radiation emitted by young stars burning exceptionally hot. Another nearby galaxy, visible below I Zwicky 18 in the image as a collection of blue stars, orbits its larger companion. Scientists suspect that its gravitational influence may trigger star formation within I Zwicky 18. The galaxy was discovered in the 1930s by Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky, from whom it gets its name. The image also reveals hundreds of other oval-shaped galaxies in the background, some white and others tinted orange because they're so far away.

author: Richard Tribou
title: Space Coast launch schedule: - Orlando Sentinel
mainText: The Space Coast set a new launch record in 2023 with 72 orbital missions from either Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. The pace of launches could ramp up by the end of 2024 to a near twice-weekly rate with as many as 111 missions possible. Check back for the latest information on upcoming launches. By The Numbers: 2024: 21 Space Coast launches in 2024 (updated March 30) | 14 from Cape Canaveral, 7 from KSC | 20 from SpaceX (20 Falcon 9s), 1 from ULA (1 Vulcan) | 2 human spaceflight ( Ax-3, Crew-8) 2023: 72 Space Coast launches in 2023 | 59 from Cape Canaveral, 13 from KSC | 68 from SpaceX (63 Falcon 9s, 5 Falcon Heavy), 3 from United Launch Alliance (1 Delta IV Heavy, 2 Atlas V), 1 from Relativity Space | 3 human spaceflights ( Crew-6, Ax-2, Crew-7) Details on past launches can be found at the end of file. This was 20th SpaceX launch from the Space Coast in 2024 and 21st among all companies. Read more. The Space Force has one more launch on a ULA Atlas V rocket before future missions transition to ULA’s new Vulcan Centaur. Read more. author: Elizabeth Weise
title: April 2024 eclipse could give scientists new data, but they need help - USA TODAY
mainText: Scientists are seeking assistance from the public to observe the effects of the total solar eclipse that will cover much of the United States on April 8, 2024. This is one of the largest natural wonders of the year. Those located inside or near the totality can participate in at least four different projects. These include observing animal behavior, photographing the sun's corona (weather permitting), and recording the soundscape of the eclipse. There are also state-level projects being organized in Indiana, Ohio, and other places. For the 2017 solar eclipse, Adam Hartstone-Rose, a professor of biological sciences at North Carolina State University, set up an experiment to observe zoo animals as darkness fell. More than two-thirds of the animals exhibited changed behavior, some of it extreme. For 2024, he's going national with the project SolarEclipseSafari.org. Volunteers will be asked to observe and report on animals near them, including pets, farm and wild animals, and record how they behave during the eclipse. People who plan to photograph the eclipse with cameras on tripods can help NASA scientists study the Sun’s outer atmosphere – the corona – which is revealed during totality. The corona is the birthplace of the solar wind, the stream of particles and material flowing from the Sun that can impact the Earth, and the best time to observe it is during a total solar eclipse. But the full eclipse, or totality, only lasts for four-and-a-half minutes at a maximum in any one place, which isn't long enough to watch the coronal change. NASA hopes to gather photographs from across the 90 minutes during which the Moon’s shadow crosses from Mexico to Canada. These will then be combined into movies that will reveal otherwise difficult-to-observe activity in the corona.

author: HT News Desk
title: Explained: NASA to launch three sounding rockets into April solar eclipse. Why? - Hindustan Times
mainText: NASA has planned to launch three sounding rockets during the total solar eclipse on April 8, from its Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia. These rockets, named Atmospheric Perturbations around Eclipse Path (APEP), will lift off 45 minutes before, during, and 45 minutes after the peak local eclipse. The next total solar eclipse in the US won't happen until 2044, according to NASA. With this strategic timing, the United States space agency aims to gather data on how the sudden dimming of sunlight during an eclipse impacts the ionosphere, causing disturbances that could disrupt communications, it said in a statement. The ionosphere, situated between 90 to 500 kilometres above the Earth's surface, is an electrified region in the atmosphere. According to mission lead Aroh Barjatya, it serves as a reflective and refractive medium for radio signals and significantly influences satellite communications as signals traverse through it. The ionosphere is like a protective layer high above Earth, acting as a barrier between our atmosphere and space. It's filled with particles that get charged up by the Sun's energy. At night, these charged particles calm down and turn neutral again. But things like Earth's weather and space events can shake up the ionosphere, making it hard to predict what it'll be like, NASA said. As the eclipse moves across the sky, it creates a quick sunset effect, causing big waves and small disturbances in the atmosphere. These disturbances mess with radio signals on various frequencies. By studying these changes, scientists can make better models to predict how our communication might get disrupted, especially on high-frequency bands, NASA said. A sounding rocket has the capability to transport scientific instruments to altitudes ranging from approximately 50 to 500 kilometres above Earth's surface. These heights are generally beyond the reach of science balloons and below the safe operating range of satellites, rendering sounding rockets the sole platforms suitable for direct measurements in these regions. The next total solar eclipse in the US won't happen until 2044, said NASA. So, these experiments are a golden chance for scientists to gather important data.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Cool Coating for a Hot Mission: NISAR's Final Preparations - SciTechDaily
mainText: NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) are preparing for the launch of the NISAR (NASA ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite, a joint Earth-observing mission. The satellite is almost ready for launch, with a launch readiness date to be determined at the end of April. The spacecraft will be launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre on India’s southeastern coast. One of the final preparations includes applying a special coating to hardware components on the satellite’s 39-foot-diameter (12-meter) radar antenna reflector, which is among NASA’s primary contributions to the mission. This coating is being added as a precautionary measure to mitigate any temperature increases that could potentially affect the deployment of the reflector. The reflector will transmit and receive microwave signals to and from Earth’s surface during science operations, enabling NISAR to scan nearly all the planet’s land and ice surfaces twice every 12 days to collect science data. The special coating being added will limit the temperature by reflecting more solar radiation off the reflector hardware. Due to the reflector’s size and complexity, it is being shipped from the ISRO site in India where the satellite is being assembled to a specialized facility in California for the application of the coating. Once the thermal performance of the coating has been fully verified, a launch readiness date will be set. When the reflector returns to India, teams from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and ISRO will integrate it onto the satellite. NISAR, the first hardware collaboration between NASA and ISRO on an Earth-observing mission, is a uniquely powerful and trailblazing satellite. By combining two kinds of synthetic aperture radars, it will offer measurements of Earth’s evolving surface – including changes in ice sheets and glaciers, wetlands and forests, and land around volcanoes and earthquake faults.

author: Kartikeya Jain
title: Kodaikanal Solar Observatory: 125 years of gazing at the brightest star in the earth’s sky - Scroll.in
mainText: The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory, located in Tamil Nadu, has been capturing images of the sun every day for over a century, starting from a small shed to numerous buildings and telescopes. The observatory is currently undertaking a digitisation project, scanning and uploading all the archives dating back to 1904. The observatory is owned and operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics. The observatory's 12-meter-high solar tower, equipped with a modern spectrograph, was set up in 1960, enabling pioneering helioseismology investigations and measurements of vector magnetic fields. The observatory's staff, including P Manikandan, also known as Sathish, are involved in digitising the photographic glass plates of the sun, along with sun charts – hand-drawings of the sun, usually in pencil, highlighting sunspots and other features. Sathish's great-grandfather, V Poomban, was hired by the British as a peon when the observatory was first set up in the early 1900s. Since then, Poomban’s son, grandson and great-grandson have all ended up working at this historic institution, either as support staff or directly assisting the scientists in observing the sun every day. The observatory has made several important observations over the years. For instance, spectroscopic observations taken during the August 18, 1868, total solar eclipse from Guntur in Andhra Pradesh led to the discovery of helium, the Universe’s second-most abundant element after hydrogen. The first dedicated solar observations were recorded later in 1878 from the Trigonometrical Survey Office in Dehradun. The observatory has a digital repository containing 1.48 lakh digitised solar images of 10 terabytes, including 33,500 white-light images (showing sunspots) and thousands of other images of the Sun recorded every day since the start of the 20th century.

author: Sandhya Ramesh
title: After a solar eruption & a ‘severe’ geomagnetic storm, an aurorae in the sky - ThePrint
mainText: At the beginning of the week, scientists reported a large coronal mass ejection, or a release of material from the sun's surface, directed towards Earth. This material interacted with Earth's atmosphere, triggering a 'severe' geomagnetic storm. The event was not significant enough to affect the public, but powerful geomagnetic storms in space can damage our satellites, the International Space Station (ISS), and on Earth, they can impact the electrical grid. This particular event resulted in beautiful aurorae observed in higher latitudes. You can read the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) report for more details. In addition to this, geologists from NASA presented the first findings from the analysis of soil samples from the asteroid Bennu. The preprint paper released this week reveals several findings about the origin of this peculiarly shaped space rock. Analysis of the particles from the asteroid's surface, which returned to Earth last year, indicates that Bennu was likely part of a wet, tectonically active planet. This planet orbited one or more stars before our sun was even born. It also contains organic molecules necessary for life, as most asteroids do. These findings lend more support to the theory that asteroids might have bombarded Earth with organic molecules and water, leading to life. Scientists studying dogs observed the brain activity of our best friends when they were asked to respond to commands. While we already know that dogs can recognize words and objects, the study managed to track brain activity for what happens when dogs are told object names. Scans revealed that dogs had more difficulty retrieving a correct item, as compared to commands to action like walk or sit, since dogs visually picture these items in their heads. They likely also replay a memory associated with objects. Another study on human brains, through a 75-year history, has shown that human brains have been getting larger and larger over the past century. People born in the 1970s had a 6.6 percent larger brain volume and 15 percent larger brain surface area than people born in the 1930s. The study was conducted over 20 years, and the findings might actually mean some good news. Larger brains could indicate improved brain health and physical development, able to delay neurodegenerative diseases like dementia and Alzheimer’s.

author: Julia Maruca
title: Don't look at the solar eclipse without proper eye protection, doctors warn - TribLIVE
mainText: The sun is about to pull another disappearing act across North America, turning day into night during a total solar eclipse on April 8. The peak spectacle will last up to 4 minutes, 28 seconds in the path of total darkness, twice as long as the total solar eclipse that dimmed U.S. skies in 2017. The moon will line up perfectly between the Earth and the sun, blotting out the sunlight. It will take less than 21/2 hours for the moon's shadow to slice a diagonal line from the southwest to the northeast across North America, briefly plunging communities along the track into darkness. Erie will be in the path of totality for nearly four minutes. The Pittsburgh region will see the moon cover approximately 97% of the sun, with maximum totality at 3:17 p.m., according to the Carnegie Science Center. Sunlight will dim for a few minutes here, but the sky will not go dark. Though it may be tempting to sneak a peek, guidance from health officials is clear: It’s not safe to view the April 8 solar eclipse without proper eye protection. The Pittsburgh region will experience a partial solar eclipse, with 95% totality at the peak about 3:15 p.m. Those to the north in Erie will see a total solar eclipse. In either area as well as across the world, UV rays from the sun will hurt your eyes if you look directly at the eclipse, said Dr. Sarah Zambotti, an Allegheny Health Network optometrist. Those interested in seeing the eclipse should use protective eclipse glasses that are supported by the American Astronomical Society. Looking for a quick second without eclipse glasses, or while using ordinary sunglasses, won’t be enough to avoid potential injury, she said. “I think the biggest misconception is that you can look at it with your bare eyes, or you can look at it for a second and look away,” she said. “It is really dangerous for you to look with your bare eyes.” Solar retinopathy, a type of eye damage that can be brought on by looking at the sun during an eclipse, can lead to permanent vision loss, said Dr. Carol Fox, chief medical officer at Independence Health System. “When you look directly at the sun, it can hit your retina and can cause permanent damage,” Fox said. “It inflames or can essentially burn the retina.” Symptoms of solar retinopathy can include blurry vision, headaches, a blind spot in the center of your vision, increased light sensitivity, distorted vision and changes in the way you see color, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. If you think you have injured your eyes by looking at the eclipse, you should call your eye doctor, Zambotti said. Symptoms can sometimes be delayed for 30 minutes or up to 24 hours. “If you are starting to have different symptoms, or you are noticing your eyes are blurry, painful, red or irritated, or you have missing vision in the center of your vision, obviously call your eye doctor right away,” Zambotti said.

author: Ian Krietzberg
title: Former NASA administrator says the space around Earth is like the 'Wild West' - TheStreet
mainText: The former NASA administrator has likened the space around Earth to the 'Wild West', highlighting the increasing congestion of space debris orbiting our planet. Currently, there are about 9,000 functional satellites in orbit, as per the European Space Agency. However, private corporations like SpaceX and Amazon have plans to launch tens of thousands more satellites. The total mass orbiting Earth exceeds 11,000 tons, with over 35,000 pieces of space debris being tracked. SpaceX alone operates around 5,000 Starlink satellites and plans to increase this number to 40,000 or more. Amazon also plans to launch around 3,000 similar satellites over the next six years as part of its Project Kuiper program. Research firm Quilty Space predicts that 20,000 new satellites will be launched by 2030. Former NASA administrator Sean O’Keefe warns that the increasing amount of space debris is an 'accident waiting to happen'. The risk of mid-orbit collisions could damage or destroy active satellites or spacecraft. The problem is compounded by the fact that spacecraft lack the option of braking and laying on the horn, as they're all traveling at 17,500 miles an hour.

author: Keith Cowing
title: Ice Planet Survey: The Changing Ice Cap of Mars - Astrobiology - Astrobiology News
mainText: The Ice Planet Survey reveals the evolving ice cap of Mars. The icy deposits at the South Pole of Mars narrate a tale of change. What remains of a once more extensive deposit made up of dry ice forms the south polar residual cap. This 'residual' cap is so named because it persists even after the much larger seasonal cap vanishes each summer. This mesa in this cutout is diminishing over time as the frozen carbon dioxide sublimates. The pits in this sheet of dry ice, which give the deposit a Swiss cheese-like appearance, are growing over time, revealing an older surface beneath that is likely composed of water ice. Unlike the shrinking ice caps on Earth, climate change is not the culprit on Mars. Even as the walls of these pits erode away, the intervening flat surfaces are accumulating new dry ice. The total quantity of frozen carbon dioxide at the South Pole may even be on the rise.

author: Martijn Luinstra
title: Event Horizon Telescope reveals magnetic fields around the Milky Way's central black hole - NASASpaceFlight.com - NASASpaceflight.com
mainText: Astronomers from the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration have discovered strong magnetic fields spiraling around the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy, known as Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*). The neatly ordered magnetic fields have similarities with those that surround the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy M87. This is surprising given that Sgr A* has a mass of around 4.3 million times that of the sun, but M87* is much larger, with a mass equivalent to around 6.5 billion suns. The new EHT observation of Sgr A* suggests that strong and well-organized magnetic fields could be common to all black holes. Also, because M87*'s magnetic fields drive powerful outflows or 'jets,' the results hint that Sgr A* could have a hidden and faint jet all of its own. The EHT is comprised of many telescopes across the globe, including the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), which come together to form an Earth-sized telescope that is no stranger to making scientific history. In 2017, the EHT captured the first image of a black hole and its environment, imaging M87* located around 53.5 million light-years from Earth. Two years after this image was revealed to the public in 2019, the EHT collaboration revealed the first look at polarized light around a black hole, M87*, once again.

author: Tessa Koumoundouros
title: A Shape Called a 'Sphinx' Could Explain Handedness in Biology - ScienceAlert
mainText: The biological structures, from DNA spirals to protein configurations, often exhibit a unique asymmetry known as chirality, characterized by a preference for left- or right-handed orientations. A new study focusing on the tessellation patterns of a geometric figure derived from triangles, known as the 'sphinx', might provide insights into the preference for certain orientations in biological systems. The study was conducted by a team of researchers from the United States and Germany, who hypothesized that the combination of geometric principles and elemental physics could be responsible for these distinct patterns observed in nature. Greg Huber, a biophysicist at Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, states that despite the Universe having no inherent bias towards any handedness, chirality is profoundly present in nature. Chiral molecules, like a pair of hands facing upward, cannot be superimposed on their mirror images regardless of rotation. This distinction has serious implications, as the reversed version of a molecule could prove detrimental when used in medicinal drugs. Chiral structures aren’t limited to organic molecules; they can also appear in minerals within biological contexts. For example, the helical form of a snail’s shell or the mineralized components within our bones demonstrate such handedness. The question lies in how crystalline chiral shapes are formed on an atomic level, which is yet another aspect of the curiosity surrounding chirality. To delve deeper into the phenomenon of chirality occurrence, particularly in the dense environments of biological systems, Huber and his associates focused on the basic two-dimensional chiral shape made from triangles called the sphinx. The sphinx shape is regarded as the smallest chiral configuration creatable with triangles. The researchers employed computational models to investigate the left and right-handedness of the sphinx shape through various tessellation patterns. Their goal, as outlined in their published paper, was to understand the statistical mechanics and reveal the inherent chiral nature within densely-packed sphinx tile systems.

author: Jack Birle
title: Arizona governor signs bill making Pluto official state planet - Washington Examiner
mainText: On March 30, 2024, Governor Katie Hobbs of Arizona signed House Bill 2477 into law, officially designating Pluto as the state planet for Arizona. The bill, which simply adds 'Pluto is the official state planet' into state code, was passed unanimously in the state House in February and passed overwhelmingly in the state Senate earlier this month. The decision to designate Pluto as the official state planet is a commemoration of its discovery in the Grand Canyon State. Pluto was discovered in 1930 by scientist Clyde Tombaugh at the Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona. For most of the 20th century, it was considered the ninth planet in the solar system. However, in 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet, reducing the number of planets in the solar system back to eight. Despite this, fans of Pluto have protested the decision and insisted it is a planet alongside the likes of Neptune and Mars. Republican state-Rep. Justin Wilmeth, who introduced the bill, said that the designation of Pluto as the official planet is meant to commemorate its discovery in the Grand Canyon State. 'That’s a major astronomical achievement and it happened here in Arizona,' Wilmeth said, 'That’s something for every single citizen of this state to be proud of and it’s why I decided to sponsor the bill.'

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: KKR-RR game on April 17 might get rescheduled - Cricbuzz
mainText: The home game of Kolkata Knight Riders at Eden on April 17, where they are scheduled to play against Rajasthan Royals, is currently uncertain. The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) is contemplating either relocating the game or rescheduling it to another day. NC State coach Kevin Keatts praised Burns Jr., stating that they had an advantage throwing the ball inside to him. Burns Jr. set the tone for NC State in its stunning upset of Duke, and his performance was instrumental in sending Duke home. He scored a mid-range bucket to open the game and gave Duke big man Kyle Filipowski a forearm shiver moments later for another basket. Then in the second half, he found another gear and carried the Pack on his back. title: Sri Lanka Achieve Humongous Test Feat, Break 48-Year-Old Massive Record - NDTV Sports
mainText: The Sri Lanka cricket team made history on the second day of their Test match against Bangladesh. They scored 531 runs in their first innings without a single batter scoring a century. This is the highest total posted by any team in the history of Test cricket where none of the batters scored 100 or more. Among the top seven Sri Lanka batters, six slammed half-centuries with Kusal Mendis top-scoring with 93 while Kamindu Mendis was unbeaten on 92. The previous record belonged to India who scored 524/9 declared against New Zealand in Kanpur back in 1976. Bangladesh were 55-1 in their first innings at stumps on the second day of the second Test after bowling Sri Lanka out for 531 in Chittagong on Sunday. Opener Zakir Hasan was unbeaten on 28 alongside nightwatchman Taijul Islam on 0 after Lahiru Kumara bowled Mahmudul Hasan Joy for 21. Sri Lanka made a record 531 runs in their first innings against Bangladesh Sunday, but Kamindu Mendis narrowly missed the feat of a third Test century in consecutive innings. Sri Lanka's total, on the second day of the second Test in Chittagong, was the highest scored in Tests without any batsman scoring a century. Mendis was 92 not out when last man Asitha Fernando was run out for a duck, leaving him eight short of what would have made him only the fourth Sri Lankan to score three centuries in consecutive innings. Mendis, who scored 102 and 164 in the first Test, struck Taijul Islam for two sixes in an over to come close to the feat. But Fernando fell short of his crease in a desperate attempt to change the strike. Apart from Mendis, who was playing only his third Test, Dhananjaya de Silva (70), Dinesh Chandimal (59), Kusal Mendis (93), Dimuth Karunaratne (86) and Nishan Madhushka (57) also scored a fifty each. Shakib Al Hasan finished with 3-110 as Sri Lanka made Bangladesh toil for nearly two days after electing to bat first. Sri Lanka resumed the second day with 314-4. De Silva, like Mendis, who also scored 102 and 108 in the first Test, raised the prospect of scoring 300 on the trot before he was dismissed in the post-lunch session. Chandimal was the only batsman to be dismissed in the first session, edging Shakib behind the stumps after making 59 runs. Khaled Ahmed trapped De Silva leg before in the first over after the lunch break. Khaled could have taken another wicket in his next if Prabath Jayasuriya was not comically dropped by three slip fielders on six. Mendis was declared caught behind on 35 off Mehidy Hasan Miraz, but the decision was reversed after review.

author: Victoria Song
title: 20 years of Gmail - The Verge
mainText: Two decades ago, Google launched its free email service Gmail with an announcement that had people wondering if it was another April Fools' Day prank by co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Page and Brin had made a tradition of rolling out outlandish ideas every April 1st not long after starting their company more than a quarter century ago. One year, Google posted a job opening for a Copernicus research center on the moon. Another year, the company said it planned to roll out a "scratch and sniff" feature on its search engine. The jokes were so consistently over-the-top that people learned to laugh them off as another example of Google mischief. Which was why Page and Brin chose to unveil something no one would believe was possible on April Fools' Day, 2004. It was Gmail, a free service boasting 1 gigabyte of storage per account, an amount that sounds almost pedestrian in an age of one-terabyte iPhones. But it sounded like a preposterous amount of email capacity back then, enough to store about 13,500 emails before running out of space compared to just 30 to 60 emails in the then-leading webmail services run by Yahoo and Microsoft. That translated into 250 to 500 times more email storage space. Besides the quantum leap in storage, Gmail also came equipped with Google's search technology so users could quickly retrieve a tidbit from an old email, photo or other personal information stored on the service. It also automatically threaded together a string of communications about the same topic so everything flowed together as if it was a single conversation. "The original pitch we put together was all about the three 'S's" — storage, search and speed," said former Google executive Marissa Mayer, who helped design Gmail and other company products before later becoming Yahoo's CEO. It was such a mind-bending concept that shortly after The Associated Press published a story about Gmail late on the afternoon of April Fools' 2004, readers began calling and emailing to inform the news agency it had been duped by Google's pranksters. "That was part of the charm, making a product that people won't believe is real. It kind of changed people's perceptions about the kinds of applications that were possible within a web browser," former Google engineer Paul Buchheit recalled during a recent AP interview about his efforts to build Gmail. It took three years to do as part of a project called "Caribou" — a reference to a running gag in the Dilbert comic strip. "There was something sort of absurd about the name Caribou, it just made make me laugh," said Buchheit, the 23rd employee hired at a company that now employs more than 180,000 people. The AP knew Google wasn't joking about Gmail because an AP reporter had been abruptly asked to come down from San Francisco to the company's Mountain View, California, headquarters to see something that would make the trip worthwhile.
