author: Matt Donnelly
title: ‘Megalopolis’: After Wild Speculation, What Exactly Is So ‘Bats—’ About Francis Ford Coppola’s Opus? - Variety
mainText: Francis Ford Coppola has made a significant comeback to directing with his new film 'Megalopolis', a passion project that has been over 20 years in the making. The film has been the subject of industry chatter since a late March screening for potential buyers. Reports this week suggested that Coppola was having difficulty securing a high-profile distribution deal for his 135-minute epic, which depicts a dystopia in the midst of an energy revolution. In response, Coppola secured a place in competition at the upcoming Cannes Film Festival, where the film hopes to change the narrative. This situation is not unlike the skepticism that initially met another of Coppola's passion projects, 'Apocalypse Now', which was initially dismissed by many as a vanity project before it screened at Cannes as a work in progress and went on to win the Palme d'Or. The fate of 'Megalopolis' and how Hollywood will deal with a film that has already sparked so many hot takes remains to be seen. Some were clearly put off and confused, calling the film 'batshit' and criticizing it for its disregard for conventional storytelling. Others were euphoric, sometimes to the point of eye-rolling, or made sincere attempts to reconcile the buzz with Coppola's larger body of work. For the most part, these impressions were vague as to why the buyers screening was so shocking. Coppola's long-awaited script is filled with ambiguous moral codes, sex, drugs, violence, and reflections on the uncertain future of America, according to multiple sources who have seen the film. These themes are explored with a star-studded cast that includes Adam Driver, Aubrey Plaza, Nathalie Emmanuel, Shia LaBeouf, Jon Voight, Dustin Hoffman, Giancarlo Esposito, and 'SNL' player Chloe Fineman. The film contains a scene involving Plaza and LaBeouf that will undoubtedly attract attention for its depiction of female pleasure. Surrounding that scene is plenty of 'orgiastic' content, involving numerous decadent party scenarios. 'Some people felt it was, 'Here's boobs, here's drugs.' But the decadence has a larger context for Coppola, it feels a bit like a cautionary tale about where America is headed,' said one viewer.

author: By Mary Gilbert, Antoinette Radford, Rachel Ramirez, Eric Zerkel, Tori B. Powell and Elise Hammond, CNN
title: Dangerous tornado and flooding situation unfolding in South: Live updates - CNN
mainText: Severe storms are currently threatening Texas and the South. Flooding and tornadoes are a significant threat, particularly in the South. The east Texas town of Kirbyville is experiencing severe flooding, with all major roads into the town shut down. The Jasper County Sheriff’s Office has issued a disaster declaration due to the flooding. The sheriff’s office has reported major flooding throughout the county, with another line of storms on the way. Multiple local fire departments are assisting with rescues, and the urban search and rescue team Texas A&M Task Force 1 is also deployed. The public school districts in the east Texas towns of Kirbyville and Port Arthur are closed due to severe flooding and damage resulting from the severe weather. The two districts have a combined enrollment of 9,654 students. Severe storms, including possible tornadoes, are hitting parts of the southern US.

author: BILL BARROW, ADRIANA GOMEZ LICON
title: Trump says Arizona's abortion ban goes too far while defending the overturning of Roe v. Wade - The Associated Press
mainText: Donald Trump, the former president, has stated that an Arizona law criminalizing nearly all abortions is excessive. He has called on Arizona lawmakers to amend it, while also defending the overturning of Roe v. Wade, which allowed states to prohibit the procedure. Trump expressed confidence that the issue would be resolved and that the governor and others would bring it back to a reasonable level. He believes this will be taken care of quickly. Trump is facing political pressure on abortion rights, which Democrats hope will be a defining issue in the upcoming November election. This comes after he released a video statement earlier this week declining to endorse a national abortion ban and stating that he believes limits should be left to the states. His earlier statement has upset religious conservatives and energized allies of President Joe Biden who view abortion rights as one of Trump's weaknesses. The Arizona Supreme Court ruling on Tuesday paved the way for the enforcement of an 1864 law that bans abortion at all stages of pregnancy with no exceptions for rape or incest. Trump maintains that he is proud that the three Supreme Court justices he nominated voted to overturn Roe v. Wade, stating that states will have different restrictions. He supports three exceptions in cases of rape, incest, and when the life of the mother is at risk. He also mentioned a Florida law that bans abortions after six weeks, suggesting that it may also change. Trump ignored questions about how he plans to vote himself on Florida’s pending state constitutional amendment that would enshrine abortion access as a right of his home state’s residents. He did not elaborate on what he thinks the level of restrictions and access should be in Arizona or any other state.

author: Venkat
title: CBN is coming with bogus report with fake promises.. - Greatandhra
mainText: YSRCP supremo YS Jagan Mohan Reddy, in response to TDP president Chandrababu Naidu's alleged dissemination of deceptive reports and promises, has emphasized his commitment to presenting tangible progress achieved during his tenure to the electorate ahead of the forthcoming elections. He contends that the extensive welfare and developmental measures implemented over the past 58 months are readily apparent to the populace, owing to numerous reforms initiated at grassroots levels. Jagan warns that a return to power by Naidu would jeopardize these schemes and reforms. He urges the public to lend their support to YSRCP to ensure the continuity of welfare initiatives and sustained development. Speaking at a significant public gathering in Piduguralla of the Gurazala constituency as part of the Memantha Sidham series, the Chief Minister underscores that the upcoming elections are not merely a contest between himself and Naidu, but a referendum on trustworthiness. He calls upon the people to unite against malevolence, obscurity, conspiracies, and deception, framing the election as pivotal for shaping their collective future and the prospects of succeeding generations. Jagan implores families to deliberate on the positive impacts of his administration over the past 58 months and make an informed choice to safeguard the continuity of these initiatives. He encourages scrutiny of Naidu's track record, highlighting unfulfilled promises made prior to the 2014 polls. Jagan contrasts this with his government's tangible support for farmers, exemplified by the YSR Rythu Bharosa scheme, which provided substantial financial aid alongside agricultural assistance. Jagan challenges Naidu's credibility by pointing out discrepancies in past claims regarding job creation. He contrasts the meager job opportunities created under Naidu's tenure with the significant employment generated by his administration. Highlighting ongoing infrastructure projects aimed at bolstering economic growth, Jagan outlines plans for new ports, industrial corridors, fishing harbors, and fish landing centers. He invites constituents to observe firsthand the developmental projects initiated by his administration, including village secretariats, Nadu-Nedu schools, hospitals, and medical colleges. Overall, Jagan underscores the imperative of electing a trustworthy and effective government committed to sustained progress and welfare for the people of the state.

author: Allison Johnson
title: Google's AI photo editing tools are expanding to a lot more phones - The Verge
mainText: Google Photos is introducing a new feature called Magic Editor, which uses generative AI to help users edit their photos. This new feature will allow users to make complex edits without needing professional editing skills. Magic Editor uses a combination of AI techniques to help users edit specific parts of an image, such as the subject, sky, or background. This gives users more control over the final look and feel of their photo. Magic Editor can also help improve the overall composition of a photo by allowing users to reposition the subject of their shot to the best spot. For example, if a user is trying to get the perfect photo from a popular waterfall, they could remove a bag strap they forgot to take off, make the sky brighter and less cloudy, and relocate and change the scale of their subject so they're perfectly lined up under the waterfall. Magic Editor can also create new content to fill in the gaps after repositioning a subject. For instance, if a user wants to make a boy on his birthday front and center in a photo, Magic Editor can create more of the bench and balloons to fill in the gaps, and they'll blend seamlessly into the photo. Google plans to give select Pixel phones early access to Magic Editor later this year. While this new technology will open up exciting editing possibilities, Google acknowledges that there might be times when the result isn't exactly what the user imagined. User feedback will be important in helping Google improve Magic Editor over time. Over the past few years, AI has simplified complex photo editing tasks, allowing users to easily enhance their memories and get creative with their editing. With Magic Editor, Google Photos is taking the editing experience to the next level.

author: Emma Tucker, Holly Yan
title: 6 ex-officers who pleaded guilty in ‘Goon Squad’ torture of 2 Black men sentenced in state court - CNN
mainText: The six former Mississippi law enforcement officers, who are members of the self-styled “Goon Squad,” received state sentences Wednesday ranging from 15 and 45 years. They had pleaded guilty in August to charges stemming from the January 2023 torture and abuse of two Black men. The state sentences are to run concurrently with their federal sentences. The officers sentenced were Brett McAlpin, Jeffrey Middleton, Daniel Opdyke, Christian Dedmon, Hunter Elward, and Joshua Hartfield. Victim statements were read in court, with Michael Jenkins stating, "Your honor, they killed me. I just didn't die," and describing how the actions of the former officers have affected his life. Eddie Parker’s statement read, “I never knew the ones that were sworn to protect and serve would be the ones that needed protection from,". Malik Shabazz, attorney for victims Michael Jenkins and Eddie Park, said today's sentencing is "significant," but added that he still hoped the former officers received more time.

author: Mark Haranas
title: Google Cloud's New AI Launches For Channel Partners At Google Next 2024 - CRN
mainText: Google Cloud has announced several new enhancements for its partners at Google Cloud Next 2024, including a new generative AI specialization and AI delivery technical bootcamps for solution providers. Kevin Ichhpurani, corporate vice president of Global Ecosystem and Channels at Google Cloud, emphasized the opportunities available to Google Cloud partners in helping customers transform with Google's expansive and open platform for AI. The company is committed to supporting its partners at every level of the AI stack, with a partner-led approach to services and delivery, growing incentives and rewards, new opportunities for training and differentiation, and optimized routes-to-market to help partners close larger deals faster, and more often. Google Cloud has increased its incentives and other channel programs by upwards of 10X for system integrators and software vendors to implement Google Cloud’s generative AI solutions. Rewards have also been doubled for services partners who drive more workload adoption and accelerate adoption of key products. Jason Geis, CEO and co-founder of Google partner CloudWerx, said the AI channel incentive increases will drive profitability in 2024. Google Cloud has launched a new Generative AI Services Specialization for partners who demonstrate the highest level of technical proficiency with Google Cloud GenAI offerings. This new specialization will unlock earlier access to Google-led GenAI projects, additional funding for generative AI assessment work, and increased access to AI resources and partner marketing funds. Google also unveiled new generative AI Delivery Excellence and Technical Bootcamps for partners at Google Cloud Next this week.

author: Breck Dumas
title: See Toyota's first 4Runner SUV in 15 years, and it is not an EV - Fox Business
mainText: Toyota unveiled its brand new 2025 4Runner this week, marking the first major update to the popular SUV in 15 years. The sixth-generation 4Runner, which will be available for sale in the U.S. in the fall, will for the first time have a hybrid version available. The new 4Runner features an all-new platform shared with the new Tacoma pickup and full-size Sequoia and Land Cruiser SUVs. The new frame adds strength and rigidity but will also help with overall comfort and handling. The new base engine is a turbocharged 4-cylinder dubbed i-Force that produces 278 horsepower and 317 lb.-ft of torque. The hybrid model, which has an i-Force MAX powertrain with an electric motor added to the gas engine, is juiced up to 326 horsepower. Both engine choices are also paired with a more modern eight-speed automatic transmission. Toyota believes hybrid powertrains will not only help vehicles like the 4Runner and the all-new 2025 Camry with performance and efficiency but also bridge the gap to full electrification in the US and abroad.

author: Rebecca Beitsch, Mychael Schnell
title: Group of Republicans blocks FISA bill with spy powers deadline looming - The Hill
mainText: On Wednesday, a group of House Republicans blocked a procedural vote to begin debate on a bill to reauthorize the nation’s warrantless surveillance powers. This move has left the chamber scrambling on how to address this important spy tool before it expires next week. Nineteen Republicans joined Democrats in voting against a rule for legislation to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), blocking the measure from advancing 193-228. This move comes after former President Trump urged Republicans to “kill FISA” on Wednesday, adding another layer of complexity to an already contentious debate. The blocked procedural vote also hampers a plan from House leadership to take up an amendment many of the GOP’s right wing say is a top priority – adding a warrant requirement to the bill. Led by Rep. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla) and other MAGA-aligned conservatives, the vote marks yet another instance of members of the GOP blocking what is typically a routine party line vote in protest of legislation. Section 702 allows the government to spy on foreigners located abroad, but that surveillance also sweeps in their communications with any Americans with whom they are in contact. The issue of whether to require a warrant to access the information on Americans caught up in the surveillance has created strange bedfellows, with some members on both sides of the aisle uniting around an amendment they see as a safeguard for Americans, and others saying it would gut the program entirely. The law is set to expire April 19 – a deadline that comes after the House was forced to pass a short-term extension of FISA 702 in December as Republicans lawmakers failed to reach agreement over competing bills from the House Judiciary and Intelligence Committees.

author: Alana Hagues
title: Prince Of Persia Roguelite From Dead Cells Dev Revealed, Switch Not Confirmed - Nintendo Life
mainText: The rumors have been confirmed — The Rogue Prince of Persia is indeed a reality, and it's being developed by the co-developer of Dead Cells, Evil Empire. This announcement was made during the Triple-i Initiative, and The Rogue Prince of Persia is set to come to Steam Early Access on 14th May 2024. As of now, no other platforms have been announced, but it is expected that when the full release is out, it will be available on Switch or a future Nintendo console. Evil Empire is combining 'challenging but accessible' platforming and incorporating the long-standing franchises into the roguelite formula to leverage the series' flashy acrobatics. The objective is to save Persia from a Hun invasion and become a hero. The game appears stunning, showcasing the signature Evil Empire art style — but this time, instead of pixels, Prince of Persia has adopted a more hand-drawn look, and it appears smooth and seamless. Game Informer has released 15 minutes of gameplay on the upcoming roguelite, so you can check out their video for more details. After being inactive for years, Ubisoft's Prince of Persia series has two game releases in a single year. In January, the franchise ventured into the Metroidvania genre with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, and Evil Empire's title will be the second game when it arrives on PC in Early Access in May. We'll keep you updated if and when The Rogue Prince of Persia is coming to Switch. In the meantime, don't forget about our Best Prince of Persia games poll, and let us know your thoughts on this title in the comments.

author: Michael Voepel
title: WNBA TV slate fixed on Fever, likely No. 1 Clark - ESPN
mainText: The WNBA TV schedule is set to focus on the Indiana Fever, who are expected to draft Iowa's Caitlin Clark as the No. 1 pick in the upcoming WNBA draft. This season, 36 out of their 40 games will be broadcasted or streamed. The news comes after Caitlin Clark confirmed her entry into the 2024 WNBA draft, solidifying her position as the definite No. 1 pick. The Indiana Fever's games being broadcasted or streamed is a significant development, as it provides increased visibility for the team and the league. The decision to focus on the Fever is likely due to the anticipation surrounding Caitlin Clark, who has been a standout player at Iowa. Her entry into the draft and potential selection by the Fever is expected to bring a lot of excitement and attention to the team. However, the broadcast schedule could change based on various factors, including team performance and player injuries.

author: Sam Fossum, Arlette Saenz, Kayla Tausche, Betsy Klein, Michael Williams
title: Biden hosts Japanese prime minister for a state visit that sends a message to China - CNN
mainText: On April 10, 2024, President Joe Biden and First Lady Jill Biden hosted Prime Minister Kishida Fumio and Mrs. Kishida Yuko of Japan for an official visit to the United States. This visit included a state dinner. The visit aimed to strengthen the critical alliance between the U.S. and Japan as the United States sought to counter China's influence in the Indo-Pacific region. During the visit, President Biden welcomed Mr. Kishida to the White House using words like timeless, monumental, and indestructible, as he described the close relationship between the U.S. and Japan. The two leaders discussed ways of forging closer economic and military ties as they sought to counter the growing influence of China in Asia and worldwide. This visit was significant as Kishida was the fifth world leader honored by Biden with a state dinner since he took office in 2021. Ahead of the White House visit, Kishida visited Arlington National Cemetery and stopped by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The prime minister was also invited to address a joint meeting of Congress on Thursday. He was just the second Japanese leader to address the body; Shinzo Abe gave a speech to Congress in 2015.

author: Haley Ott
title: Hamas says Israeli airstrike kills 3 sons of the group's political leader Ismail Haniyeh in Gaza - CBS News
mainText: On April 10, 2024, three sons of Hamas' most senior political leader, Ismail Haniyeh, were killed in an Israeli airstrike in the Gaza Strip. The sons, Ameer, Hazem, and Mohammed Haniyeh, were killed near the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City. The strike hit a vehicle near a home belonging to the Haniyeh family. Haniyeh himself acknowledged the death of more family members, and he warned Israel that it would not "break the resolve of our people." He also stated that a number of his grandchildren were also killed, and the group had been targeted when they were visiting relatives for Eid. Haniyeh said, "The occupation thinks that by targeting sons of the leaders, they will break the resolve of our people,". He further added, "We will not retreat, and we are going to go all the way to liberate Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa." Haniyeh said 60 members of his family had been killed since Israel launched its war in Gaza against Hamas, which was sparked by the group's bloody Oct. 7 terror attack.

author: Jeff Cox
title: Fed wants more confidence that inflation is moving toward 2% target, meeting minutes indicate - CNBC
mainText: Federal Reserve officials at their March meeting expressed concern that inflation wasn’t moving lower quickly enough, though they still expected to cut interest rates at some point this year. At a meeting in which the Federal Open Market Committee again voted to hold short-term borrowing rates steady, policymakers also showed misgivings that inflation, while easing, wasn’t doing so in a convincing enough fashion. The Fed currently targets its benchmark rate between 5.25%-5.5%. As such, FOMC members voted to keep language in the post-meeting statement that they wouldn’t be cutting rates until they “gained greater confidence” that inflation was on a steady path back to the central bank’s 2% annual target. “Participants generally noted their uncertainty about the persistence of high inflation and expressed the view that recent data had not increased their confidence that inflation was moving sustainably down to 2 percent,” the minutes said. In what apparently was a lengthy discussion about inflation at the meeting, officials said geopolitical turmoil and rising energy prices remain risks that could push inflation higher. They also cited the potential that looser policy could add to price pressures. On the downside, they cited a more balanced labor market, enhanced technology along with economic weakness in China and a deteriorating commercial real estate market. U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell holds a press conference following a two-day meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on interest rate policy in Washington, U.S., March 20, 2024. They also discussed higher-than-expected inflation readings in January and February. Chair Jerome Powell said it’s possible the two months’ readings were caused by seasonal issues, though he added it’s hard to tell at this point. There were members at the meeting who disagreed. “Some participants noted that the recent increases in inflation had been relatively broad based and therefore should not be discounted as merely statistical aberrations,” the minutes stated. That part of the discussion was partly relevant considering the release came the same day that the Fed received more bad news on inflation. The consumer price index, a popular inflation gauge though not the one the Fed most closely focuses on, showed a 12-month rate of 3.5% in March. That was both above market expectations and represented an increase of 0.3 percentage point from February, giving rise to the idea that hot readings to start the year may not have been an aberration. Following the CPI release, traders in the fed funds futures market recalibrated their expectations.

author: TOI News Desk
title: Looking forward to meeting with PM Modi, says Elon Musk - The Times of India
mainText: Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla, announced on Wednesday that he will be visiting India in the coming month to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Musk expressed his anticipation for the meeting on X, formerly known as Twitter, stating, "Looking forward to meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in India!". The billionaire is reportedly expected to meet PM Modi in the week of April 22 in New Delhi. This visit comes at a time when India is heading into a two-month-long election with nearly a billion voters, starting April 19, in which PM Modi is widely seen winning a rare third term. A Tesla investment announcement during the election would bolster the business-friendly credentials of PM Modi, who has for years courted foreign companies to set up manufacturing operations in India and create jobs. Musk and PM Modi last met in New York in June, and Tesla for months lobbied India to lower import taxes on electric vehicles while it weighed up a factory there. India last month unveiled a new EV policy lowering import taxes to 15% from 100% on some models if a manufacturer invests at least $500 million and sets up a factory too.

author: Sophia Abene
title: Understanding, addressing infection on Youth HIV Awareness Day - Contemporary Pediatrics
mainText: On Youth HIV Awareness Day, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) emphasizes the importance of HIV awareness and testing among young people. In the United States, a significant portion of new HIV diagnoses involves individuals between the ages of 13 and 24, which underscores the need for awareness and testing. Despite the urgency, only a small percentage of high school students have undergone HIV testing, highlighting a gap in prevention efforts. The lack of awareness is particularly concerning, as many young people are unaware of their HIV status. This unawareness prevents them from accessing preventive resources or necessary medical treatment to manage the virus effectively. Medical treatment for HIV aims to reduce the virus levels to undetectable amounts, allowing individuals to lead healthy lives. This highlights the crucial need for testing, which not only helps connect youth to preventive measures and vital health services if they test positive but also aids in the prevention of further spread of the virus. Recent trends indicate a decrease in sexual risk behaviors among high school students, including a reduction in those who are sexually active and those who have ever had sexual intercourse. However, a decline in condom use and the impact of substance use on engaging in high-risk behaviors increase the vulnerability to HIV and STDs. Certain groups, including LGBQ+ youth, face higher risks and negative health outcomes, emphasizing the need for targeted support and interventions. Schools play an important role in educating students about HIV and promoting behaviors that reduce the risk of infection. By implementing prevention programs, schools can impact students' health choices and behaviors. The CDC supports these efforts through its adolescent and school health program, reaching students and emphasizing primary prevention within the education system. To combat HIV effectively, young individuals must take steps, including educating themselves about HIV, engaging in open conversations about sexual health, and undergoing regular HIV testing as recommended by the CDC. For those who test positive, they should seek treatment, adhere to medical advice for their health, and prevent the spread of the virus.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Why public health experts are worried about bird flu - Salon
mainText: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a health alert last week about a confirmed case of H5N1 in a human. In late March, a worker on a commercial dairy farm in Texas developed a case of pink eye and later tested positive for the highly pathogenic avian influenza Type A H5N1, also known as "bird flu" or avian flu. Though the farm worker had no symptoms other than eye inflammation and wasn't hospitalized, they were isolated and received an antiviral treatment, according to the CDC. The public health agency suspects the patient got infected from a sick dairy cow. While bird flu is nothing new, this is the first time officials have confirmed that the virus has jumped from a cow to a human, and the line of transmission suggests it's easily transmitted between cows. The last time a human tested positive for H5N1 was in April 2022 in Colorado, when an individual got infected from poultry. The fact that it jumped from cattle to human is unsettling, experts say, and a cause for alarm. But not necessarily because H5N1 will turn into a pandemic this year. "There's a lot we don't know," virologist Dr. Angela Rasmussen told Salon. "We don't know essentially what kind of risk the cows themselves present." It seems "clear" that cows can present a risk to each other, Rasmussen elaborated, but what kind of a risk this poses to cow health isn't completely understood. And neither is what kind of a risk this poses to human health. In birds, HPAI is highly contagious and deadly. The big concern is that the more it jumps from animal to animal, or animal to human, the more likely it is to mutate to better infect humans. Of course, RNA viruses like influenza and SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19, are always mutating. Every replication in a hosts' cells presents a chance for a mutation to emerge. While viruses technically aren't alive, it's their nature to mutate and evolve as they infect hosts' cells and replicate. This is how they reproduce. Thus, understanding how H5N1 in mutating is critical in assessing the potential risk to both animal and human health and how close the U.S. could be to a bird flu pandemic. Fortunately, bird flu doesn't appear to be jumping from human to human, public health officials say. According to the CDC, the current risk these viruses pose to the public remains low.

author: PTI
title: Physical activity in evening linked to greatest health benefits for obese, diabetic: Study - Deccan Herald
mainText: Undertaking most of the daily physical activity in the evening is linked to the greatest health benefits for people suffering from obesity and diabetes, new research has found. According to the study published in the journal Diabetes Care, those performing a majority of their "out-of-breath" vigorous activity between 6 pm and midnight were found to have the lowest risk of dying prematurely and from cardiac ailments. The study followed nearly 30,000 people aged 40 years or above over almost eight years. "Exercise is by no means the only solution to the obesity crisis. But this research does suggest that people who can plan their activity into certain times of the day may best offset some of these health risks," said lead author Angelo Sabag, a lecturer in exercise physiology at The University of Sydney, Australia. Using wearable devices, the participants' physical activity was recorded, along with the time of the day when it was undertaken. The researchers did not just track structured exercise, but also moderate to vigorous aerobic activity performed in bouts of three minutes or more, as they said previous research has shown such activity to be strongly associated with glucose control and lowering the risk of heart-related diseases. "We didn't discriminate on the kind of activity we tracked. It could be anything from power walking to climbing the stairs, but could also include structured exercise such as running, occupational labour or even vigorously cleaning the house," said Matthew Ahmadi, a postdoctoral research fellow at The University of Sydney. The frequency with which such activity was performed was found to be more important than the total amount of physical activity undertaken throughout the entire day. Even though the findings are observational with no cause-and-effect links established, the researchers said it supports the original hypothesis that people living with diabetes or obesity, and are already glucose intolerant in the late evening, may be able to offset some of that intolerance by performing physical activity in the evening.

author: Deb Balzer, Mayo Clinic News Network
title: Oncologist suggests three ways to prevent head and neck cancer - Medical Xpress
mainText: Dr. Katharine Price, a medical oncologist with the Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, suggests three ways to reduce risks and help prevent head and neck cancer. These include avoiding tobacco use, minimizing alcohol consumption, and getting vaccinated for HPV. Tobacco and alcohol use are significant risk factors for head and neck cancer, and their combined use can further increase this risk. On the other hand, HPV is responsible for about 70% of head and neck cancers. These cancers have a different biology and are more treatable, meaning they respond better to treatments and tend to have a higher cure rate. Therefore, Dr. Price emphasizes the importance of HPV vaccination. In addition to these preventive measures, Dr. Price also encourages maintaining a healthy diet. A whole-food diet, with minimal processed foods and refined sugars, is recommended.

author: Amy Eisinger
title: Exercise at night for biggest benefit — if you fall into this group - New York Post
mainText: A new study suggests that getting the majority of your exercise at night might actually be the most beneficial when it comes to living a longer life. Researchers in Australia, who published their work in the journal Diabetes Care, looked at data from nearly 30,000 people over eight years and found that for those living with obesity, nighttime movement between the hours of 6 p.m. and midnight tended to be the most beneficial. The researchers noted that any type of moderate to vigorous physical activity counted — it didn't have to be a traditional sweat session. As long as you were getting your heart rate up, and getting breathless for a few minutes, it counted. Just three minutes of getting out of breath was found to hold some benefit. The researchers revealed that the frequency with which people undertook those short bouts of exercise seemed to be more important than their total amount of physical activity daily. In other words, getting your heart rate up for several minutes throughout your day might be better than one longer exercise session, followed by sitting in an office chair for the next eight hours. Using wearable devices to track movement, researchers collected data from UK Biobank for 29,836 adults over the age of 40 who were living with obesity. Nearly 3,000 of the participants also had Type 2 diabetes. The study participants wore their activity trackers nonstop for seven days, and researchers categorized their movement as being primarily in the morning, afternoon or evening. Then, researchers tracked what happened to those individuals over the next eight years. They monitored for deaths, major cardiac events (like a heart attack) and microvascular events. The researchers accounted for a number of lifestyle factors, including smoking, alcohol consumption, fruit and vegetable intake, sedentary time; plus other attributes like education levels, sex and age.

author: Aadya+Jha
title: 10 non-dairy foods that help build and maintain strong bones - The Times of India
mainText: Keeping your bones strong and healthy is crucial for overall well-being, and getting enough calcium which is 700mg per day is a key factor. Here are 10 non-dairy foods that can assist in building and maintaining strong bones: 1. **Chia seeds**: These tiny seeds are packed with nutrients, including calcium. Just 100 grams of chia seeds contain a whopping 631 milligrams of calcium, making them an excellent addition to your diet for bone health. 2. **Soybeans**: Soybeans are a fantastic source of calcium. With 277 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, soybeans are a great choice for those looking to boost their bone strength. 3. **Kidney beans**: Beans are not only rich in protein and fibre but also in calcium. One hundred grams of kidney beans provide approximately 143 milligrams of calcium, making them a valuable addition to any bone-healthy diet. 4. **Sunflower seeds**: Snack on some sunflower seeds for a calcium boost! With 78 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, these seeds offer a crunchy and nutritious way to support bone health. 5. **Spinach**: This leafy green is not only rich in iron but also in calcium, with 99 milligrams per 100 grams. Adding spinach into your meals can contribute to stronger bones. 6. **Broccoli**: With 47 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, broccoli is a versatile and tasty addition to any meal. 7. **Boiled eggs**: Eggs are not just for breakfast; they're also a good source of calcium. Boiled eggs contain approximately 50 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, making them a convenient option for bone health. 8. **Almonds**: About 30 grams of almonds provide around 80 milligrams of calcium, making them a convenient way to support bone strength. 9. **Okra (Bhindi)**: One cup of okra contains about 88 milligrams of calcium, along with other essential nutrients. 10. **Oranges**: With 40 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, oranges are a juicy way to help keep your bones strong. Adding these non-dairy foods into your diet can help ensure that you're getting enough calcium to support bone health. Whether you're vegan, lactose intolerant, or simply looking to diversify your sources of calcium, these foods help build and maintain strong bones.

author: Eric W. Dolan
title: Researchers identify how eating a Western diet impairs memory functioning - PsyPost
mainText: A recent study has shed light on how early consumption of a Western diet, characterized by high levels of processed foods, saturated fats, and simple sugars, can lead to lasting deficits in hippocampal-dependent episodic memory, despite not causing obesity or metabolic dysfunction. This research emphasizes the critical role that diet plays in brain health, particularly during early developmental stages, and points towards acetylcholine signaling in the hippocampus as a potential mediator of these long-lasting memory impairments. The findings have been published in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity. Previous research has found a connection between the consumption of a Western diet and various cognitive issues. However, what remained elusive was the mechanisms that could explain how these dietary habits lead to specific cognitive detriments, such as memory loss. The new study was motivated by the broader goal of contributing actionable insights into public health strategies aimed at preventing cognitive decline. To explore the long-term effects of an early life Western diet on cognitive functions, the researchers turned to male Sprague Dawley rats, which were chosen for their well-documented responses in dietary and cognitive research. The study commenced when the rats were on postnatal day 25, a critical period for development. The dietary regimen was designed to closely mimic the nutritional profile of a Western diet, characterized by high fat, high sugar, and processed foods. To achieve this, the researchers used a cafeteria-style diet model, providing rats with free-choice access to various high-fat, high-sugar foods, and drinks, alongside standard chow for control animals. The researchers found that rats fed a Western diet during early development exhibited significant, long-lasting deficits in hippocampal-dependent episodic memory, which disruptions in hippocampal acetylcholine signaling acting as a potential mediator. Acetylcholine is a critical neurotransmitter for learning and memory processes, and its disruption has been linked to cognitive decline and conditions like Alzheimer’s disease. In the Western diet-fed rats, there were notable changes in acetylcholine neurotransmission within the hippocampus, including altered dynamics of acetylcholine release during memory tasks and long-term reductions in cholinergic tone. These findings point to a significant role of acetylcholine signaling in the observed cognitive deficits, suggesting that dietary influences on this neurotransmitter system could underlie the lasting memory impairments.

author: Rudi Kinsella
title: Worrying figures show STD rates skyrocket among Americans 55 and older - Irish Star
mainText: Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) are on the rise among Americans aged 55 and older, according to recent reports. This alarming trend has prompted U.S. health officials to call for new prevention and treatment efforts. Infections rates for some STDs, including gonorrhea and syphilis, have been rising for years. Last year, the rate of syphilis cases reached its highest since 1991, and the total number of cases hit its highest since 1948. HIV cases are also on the rise, up 16% last year. David Harvey, executive director of the National Coalition of STD Directors, called the situation “out of control”. Officials are working on new approaches to the problem, such as home-test kits for some STDs that will make it easier for people to learn they are infected and to take steps to prevent spreading it to others. Another expert said a core part of any effort must work to increase the use of condoms. "It’s pretty simple. More sexually transmitted infections occur when people are having more unprotected sex,” said Dr. Mike Saag, an infectious disease expert at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

author: Pia Araneta
title: Perimenopause is 'more than just hot flashes' — Canadian women open up about body aches, depression & migraines - Yahoo Canada Shine On
mainText: Perimenopause is a phase that often goes unrecognized because its symptoms can mimic those of other conditions. It's the transitional period before menopause, during which levels of estrogen, a key female hormone, start to decrease. You may begin having menopause-like symptoms, such as hot flashes or irregular periods. Perimenopause can last six years or more for some women. And though many might know about symptoms like hot flashes, there are many symptoms like muscle and joint pain, insomnia, and sex issues that aren't on people’s radar. When Kathleen Gillespie was 47, she was hit with a sudden wave of symptoms that left her confused and desperate for answers. She had joint pain in her knees, accompanied by a cracking sound and "shooting pain," which prevented her from being able to walk. She was suddenly unable to digest certain foods, like dairy products, which she had never had an issue with before. Her skin also became hyper-sensitive. Though there were no redness or bumps, she would put a cotton sheet on her leg and it would feel like it was burning. "My body was breaking down really quickly and I thought I was coming down with some bizarre disease," Gillespie said. Her doctor couldn't find any explanation for her symptoms. Treating each issue one by one, Gillespie was thought to have a potential food allergy, was taking 13 different prescriptions and was talking about getting her knees replaced. "I felt absolutely ashamed. It was humiliating," said Gillespie, a Vancouver resident who was living a fairly active lifestyle prior. "I had to pull back on a lot of things like doing yoga or being able to sit on the floor with my child. And it all ended up being related to my hormones." Gillespie eventually found out her symptoms all derived from being in perimenopause. After receiving menopause hormone therapy, her symptoms cleared up within weeks.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Summer Foods That Help Control Blood Sugar Levels - NDTV
mainText: The article discusses the importance of controlling blood sugar levels for overall health, particularly for individuals with diabetes or those at risk of developing diabetes. It provides a list of 10 summer foods that can help control blood sugar levels. These include berries, leafy greens, tomatoes, avocado, cucumbers, zucchini, bell peppers, watermelon, summer squash, and green beans. Each food is discussed in detail, explaining how its specific nutritional content contributes to blood sugar control. For example, berries are rich in fibre, antioxidants, and polyphenols, which slow down the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, leading to more stable blood sugar levels. Similarly, leafy greens are low in carbohydrates and calories but high in fibre, vitamins, and minerals, helping to slow down the digestion of carbohydrates and improve insulin sensitivity.

author: https://www.facebook.com/Health/
title: Study: Eating an Avocado Daily Linked to a Better Diet - Health.com
mainText: The study, published in Current Developments in Nutrition, found that people with abdominal obesity who ate one avocado per day for 26 weeks developed a higher-quality diet. After six months of daily avocado consumption, subjects' diets fell more in line with healthy eating patterns, such as those outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans. The study was not originally focused on avocados' effects on diet quality but on the effect of daily avocado intake on central obesity. However, the researchers found that daily avocado intake did not increase or decrease weight or belly fat. Instead, a secondary analysis revealed that daily avocado consumption affected another important metric: diet quality. Participants were asked to recall what they'd eaten in the past 24 hours at four different points throughout the study period. The researchers found that eating one whole avocado each day is associated with better diet quality. Avocado consumption had no effect on participants’ weight or belly fat, but it did help people reduce their sodium intake and eat more healthy fats, among other health benefits.

author: HT News Desk
title: 9.4-foot space horror! This asteroid set to get as close as 18700 km to Earth today, says NASA - Hindustan Times
mainText: A 9.2-foot asteroid, named 2024 GJ2, is set to come uncomfortably close to Earth today, according to NASA. The US space agency keeps track of all near-Earth asteroids that wander anywhere close and one that is coming today, is going to get horrifically near to our planet. The reason why a wary eye is kept on the asteroids that get too close to Earth for comfort is to know well in time whether they will get any closer or whether they have any chance of actually crashing onto our planet. Notably, a planet the size of Earth has a pretty strong gravitational pull and this can actually tug these space rocks ever-closer. The latest such horror has been dubbed as Asteroid 2024 GJ2. NASA says an asteroid that is under 10 feet is set to make a close approach to Earth today. Asteroid 2024 GJ2 NASA has revealed that this is just a small 9.4-foot asteroid, but the problem is that it has strayed too far near the Earth. For perspective, just know that this asteroid is as big as a car. The closest that this asteroid is expected to come to our planet is 18700 km. The Moon is as far away as 385,000 kilometers from Earth. This means it will come much closer than even our Moon!

author: Trisha Sengupta
title: NASA captures mysterious ‘surfboard-shaped’ object orbiting moon. Can you guess what it is - Hindustan Times
mainText: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), a spacecraft that has been studying the Moon for 15 years, captured an image of a 'surfboard-shaped' object orbiting the Moon. The image sparked conversations on social media due to its mysterious nature. Some even compared the object to the surfboard of the fictional character Silver Surfer. The object, according to NASA, is the Danuri lunar orbiter of the Korea Aerospace Research Institute. The image was captured by the LRO as it passed Danuri in opposite directions. Despite the camera exposure time being very short, only 0.338 milliseconds, Danuri appears smeared to 10 times its size in the opposite direction of travel due to the high relative travel velocities between the two spacecraft. The image and other pictures of Danuri captured by the LRO were shared by a user, prompting varied reactions. Some users joked about the image, with comments ranging from 'It's my portal. I was wondering where I left it,' to 'Aliens, what else? There is no way there can be any possible explanation for that pixel shift.'

author: HT News Desk
title: Russian spacecraft comes within 10m of destroying U.S. Satellite, NASA ‘shocked’ - Hindustan Times
mainText: On February 28, a Russian spacecraft named Timed came alarmingly close to a U.S. satellite, passing within a mere 10 meters in space. This near-miss incident could have had serious implications, potentially endangering lives on Earth. NASA's Timed satellite, which has been monitoring Earth's atmosphere, narrowly escaped a collision with the decommissioned Russian spy satellite Cosmos 2221. The incident was described as 'really scary' by Colonel Pam Melroy, NASA's deputy administrator and a former astronaut. She expressed her shock at the Space Foundation’s Space Symposium in Colorado, stating that the path ended up being less than 10 meters apart. She warned that a collision would have resulted in debris generation, with tiny shards traveling at 10,000 miles per hour, posing a risk to other spacecraft and potentially human lives. She highlighted the danger posed by even small objects in space, saying, 'It’s kind of sobering to think that something that’s the size of the eraser on the end of your pencil could wreak such havoc – but it can. We’re all worried about this. Timed really scared us.' Meanwhile, Russian space officials confirmed an ongoing air leak from the Russian segment of the International Space Station (ISS). However, they assured that it doesn't pose any danger to the crew. The Roscosmos state corporation stated that specialists are monitoring the leak and the crew regularly works to locate and repair possible leak spots.

author: Universe Today
title: NASA Spots Surfboard-Shaped Object Speeding Past The Moon - ScienceAlert
mainText: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), launched in 2009, has been mapping the lunar surface in detail, identifying potential landing sites, resources, and interesting features like lava tubes. The mission has been a success, mapping about 98.2% of the lunar surface, excluding the deeply shadowed regions in the polar areas. Recently, the LRO team captured images of another satellite speeding over the lunar surface. The Republic of Korea, or South Korea, launched their Danuri lunar orbiter in August 2022. It's the nation's first lunar orbiter, and its mission is to develop and test technologies – including the space internet – and make a topographic map of the lunar surface. The map will help select future landing sites and identify resources such as uranium, helium-3, silicon, aluminum, and water ice. Danuri carries a suite of instruments, including a spectrometer, a magnetometer, and different cameras. Significantly, it contains a camera that will allow it to image the shadowed polar regions beyond the LRO's capabilities. NASA contributed to the Korea Aerospace Research Institute's (KARI) Danuri mission. NASA built the Shadowcam instrument that images the shadowed regions at the lunar poles. As a sort of high-five to their fellow space-faring nation, the LRO captured images of Danuri as it sped by under the LRO. On March 5th and 6th, the pair of orbiters sped by each other at a combined velocity of 11,500 km/h (7,200 mp/h). There were three orbits that put the LRO in a position to capture images of the swiftly moving Danuri. During each orbit, the vertical separation between the two was different. The LRO was 5 km (3 miles) above Danuri in the first image. The LRO had to change its angle. To catch Danuri, it had to aim 43 degrees down from its usual angle. On the second orbit, only 4 km (2.5 miles) separated the pair of orbiters. During the second orbit, the LRO captured this image of Danuri from only 4 km (2.5 miles) above it. The LRO was oriented 25 degrees toward the South Korean orbiter. On the third and final orbit, the separation between the two spacecraft was greater: 8 km (5 miles.) This time, the LRO was oriented at a 60-degree angle.

author: FOX Weather
title: Astronauts' eerie view of the solar eclipse shown in insane video - New York Post
mainText: On Monday, during the total solar eclipse, astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) had an eerie view as the Moon’s shadow raced across the planet’s surface. The wait for totality on Earth took more than an hour after the partial eclipse began, but the view from low-Earth orbit provided context for how fast the Moon’s shadow is moving. According to NASA, the eclipse shadow travels at 1,100 mph at the equator and up to 5,000 mph near the poles. The astronauts living and working on the ISS orbit the Earth about every 90 minutes, witnessing 16 sunrises and sunsets in 24 hours and up to five eclipses a year. On Monday, the astronauts could not only see the eclipse as the Moon blocked the face of the Sun, but also the Moon’s shadow down on Earth as it blocked the sunlight over the path of totality – looking like a floating black hole on Earth down below. The ISS wasn’t the only view of the solar eclipse from space. SpaceX founder Elon Musk shared a video, which was taken by a Starlink satellite in low-Earth orbit. The video shows the Moon’s umbra or shadow as it moves across the planet. While the Moon was moving in front of the Sun’s face, solar and Earth-observing spacecraft recorded the eclipse in real time. The Moon’s shadow is pictured covering portions of Quebec and New Brunswick and the American state of Maine in this photograph from the International Space Station. The International Space Station soared into the solar eclipse from 261 miles above. NOAA’s GOES-East satellite tracked the Moon’s shadow moving across the Pacific Ocean and North America while the European Space Agency’s Proba-2 satellite recorded the eclipse looking toward the Sun.

author: Robert Lea
title: Why Peter Higgs leaves a massive legacy in the field of physics - Space.com
mainText: On April 8, 2024, British theoretical physicist Peter Ware Higgs passed away at the age of 94. Almost 12 years ago, on July 4, 2012, in a lecture hall in Geneva, Switzerland, Higgs became an iconic figure in modern science when it was announced that collisions between particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) facility revealed the existence of the Higgs Boson. The discovery of the Higgs boson, named for Higgs himself, has been vital for the field of particle physics. It was the last occupant of the particle zoo that's needed to complete what's known as the "Standard Model of particle physics," the best description we have of the universe on the smallest of scales. For Higgs, born in Newcastle upon Tyne in the U.K. to a Scottish mother and an English father on May 29, 1929, the moment was met with an outflow of emotion. This was unsurprising, given that this announcement represented the culmination of five decades of his work, and validated a theory that he refused to give up on. Beyond the culmination of the Standard Model, the discovery of the Higgs boson signaled the need for physicists to begin exploring physics beyond parameters they were used to, thus setting the course for physics for decades to come. "Peter Higgs' contribution to modern physics is absolutely outstanding," Luz Ángela García Peñaloza, a cosmologist at Universidad ECCI in Colombia told Space.com. "His work on quantum field theory led to a theory for which, later on, he would be awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics and explains the mechanism that provides fundamental particles with mass. He was way ahead of his time."

author: Katherine Worsham
title: Expect a sonic boom from the next SpaceX launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base - KSBY News
mainText: SpaceX is planning to launch a Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Thursday, April 11. The launch is expected to cause a sonic boom that will be heard locally. The U.S. Space Force (USSF)-62 Weather System Follow-on – Microwave (WSF-M) space vehicle was successfully transported on April 9, 2024, to the Space Launch Complex-4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, in preparation for its upcoming launch into low Earth orbit. The launch lifted off at 7:25 a.m. on Thursday morning. Shortly after, a loud sonic boom was heard by those living near Vandenberg when the rocket's first-stage booster landed back on base. The launch marked the first time SpaceX used flight-proven fairings for a National Security Space Launch (NSSL) mission. The Falcon 9 rocket will deliver the U.S. Space Force's Weather System Follow-on -- Microwave (WSF-M) satellite to low Earth orbit. The satellite will provide essential weather data, such as ocean surface wind speed and direction, ice thickness, snow depth, and soil moisture. The data will be used in military mission planning and operations. If the launch is scrubbed, SpaceX has a backup opportunity available at the same time on Friday.

author: Passant Rabie
title: Rare 'Glory' Effect Spotted on Chaotic Alien World That Rains Iron - Gizmodo
mainText: The European Space Agency’s Cheops satellite has detected signs of the ‘glory effect’ on an exoplanet for the first time, spotting colorful rings of light on WASP-76b. This phenomenon, known as a glory, occurs when light passes between water droplets in clouds or fog, creating an optical effect that resembles a rainbow halo. The reason no glory has been seen before outside our Solar System is that it requires very specific conditions. Firstly, you need atmospheric particles that are almost perfectly spherical, completely uniform, and stable enough to be observed over a long period of time. The planet’s nearby star needs to shine directly at it, with the observer – in this case, Cheops – at just the right orientation. WASP-76b is a peculiar world. The exoplanet orbits a star that’s 50% more massive and 500 degrees Celsius hotter than the Sun. WASP-76b is tidally locked to its star, meaning that one side is permanently bathed in light and intense heat. It sits around 12 times closer than Venus orbits the Sun. This extreme position has heated the planet’s atmosphere to 2,000 degrees C, causing it to expand to almost six times the volume of Jupiter (it’s nearly twice as wide but with less mass). And it also happens to rain iron on WASP-76b. Due to the difference in temperature between the day and night side, iron melts on the planet’s day side and condenses into clouds when it reaches the darker, cooler night side. Choeps, or the Characterising ExOplanet Satellite, has been observing WASP-76b for three years and has detected a surprising increase in the amount of light coming from the boundary where night meets day. “This discovery leads us to hypothesise that this unexpected glow could be caused by a strong, localised and anisotropic (directionally dependent) reflection – the glory effect,” said Olivier Demangeon, an astronomer at the Institute of Astrophysics and Space Sciences in Portugal and lead author of a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics. The scientists will still need to gather more evidence that this extra light really is the glory effect, and they plan to use an instrument on board the Webb Space Telescope to do so. ESA’s upcoming Ariel mission, which is set to launch in 2029 to create the first chemical survey of exoplanets, could also be used to prove the rare phenomenon on WASP-76b.

author: Joe Rao
title: See Jupiter close to a crescent moon (Mars near Saturn, too) in the 'View a Planet Day' night sky - Space.com
mainText: On April 10, 2024, an unofficial 'View a Planet Day' was observed, where two planets appeared very close to each other in the early morning hours, and later that same day, in the early evening sky, Jupiter was seen hovering near a slender waxing crescent moon. This created an eye-catching sight. Other celestial objects were also visible among the brightest planets in the night sky. Mars and Saturn were visible about 30 to 40 minutes before sunrise, low near the east-southeast horizon. Both planets were practically the same in brightness, separated by just a mere .02 magnitude. Saturn, the brighter (magnitude +1.14) shone sedately below Mars (magnitude +1.16), the two worlds being separated by just a half-degree, which is equal to the apparent width of the moon. The actual closest approach to each other, a little over four-tenths of a degree, came after sunrise for much of North America. If unsettled weather denied you a view of this duo on Wednesday, April 10, they appeared almost the same distance apart on the following morning, though Mars had shifted to the upper left of Saturn. If you used a telescope equipped with a low-power eyepiece, you would have been able to fit both planets into the same field of view. Along with the fact that they're virtually the same brightness, their contrast in colors was quite striking, with Mars glowing with a pumpkin hue compared to the golden-yellow Saturn.

author: Jennifer Nalewicki
title: NASA spacecraft snaps mysterious 'surfboard' orbiting the moon. What is it? - Livescience.com
mainText: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) captured images of a surfboard-shaped object near the moon, which turned out to be South Korea's lunar orbiter, Danuri. This encounter between the two spacecraft occurred as they orbited the moon in nearly parallel paths, according to NASA officials. The event took place over March 5 and 6, and due to the high speed difference between the LRO and Danuri — approximately 7,200 mph (11,500 km/h) — Danuri appeared elongated in the images, resembling a surfboard, a Live Science report said. The unique photographic opportunity was seized by the LRO operations team at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. Despite the challenge posed by the LRO's camera, which has a very short exposure time of about 0.338 milliseconds, the team managed to capture images of Danuri. This marks a significant achievement as Danuri is the first Korean spacecraft to enter lunar orbit, having done so in December 2022. The stretching effect in the images, caused by the speed difference, made Danuri look "smeared to 10 times its size," according to NASA. However, Danuri is actually a box-shaped spacecraft equipped with solar panels on each side, not resembling a surfboard in reality. Paul Byrne, an associate professor of planetary science at Washington University in St Louis, shared some of the images on social media, clarifying that Danuri's appearance as a "weirdly thin load of pixels" was a result of the high speeds involved and the camera's specifications. This incident has sparked comparisons to the Silver Surfer, a fictional character in the Marvel Universe, due to the object's surfboard-like appearance in the photos.

author: Robert Lea
title: What happened when the moon 'turned itself inside out' billions of years ago? - Space.com
mainText: Over 4.2 billion years ago, the moon underwent a transformation that turned it 'inside out,' creating the lunar surface that we are familiar with today. The moon was formed around 4.5 billion years ago when a massive body in the solar system collided with Earth, ejecting molten material into space that eventually coalesced to form our natural satellite. The subsequent evolution of the moon, however, has been described as a 'choose-your-own-adventure novel' by a team of scientists from the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory (LPL). They suggest that there are numerous potential paths that the moon could have taken to fully form, leading to the moon-Earth system that we observe today. The team proposes that one of the major events that might have shaped the moon was a period when the moon 'flipped inside out.' This theory, if true, could also solve a lingering mystery about the moon's composition. The researchers suggest that rock samples collected during the Apollo mission may indicate that there was a time when the moon 'flipped inside out.' This result, if true, might also solve a lingering mystery about the moon's composition.

author: Bryce Gray
title: 'Light waves' danced just before eclipse in Missouri. Scientists had waited years for them. - St. Louis Post-Dispatch
mainText: On April 8, 2024, a total solar eclipse occurred, and scientists in Missouri had been waiting for years to observe a particular phenomenon associated with it. Just before the eclipse, 'light waves' were seen dancing in the sky. This event was significant because it provided a unique opportunity for scientists to study the interaction of light with the Earth's atmosphere under the rare conditions created by a solar eclipse. The phenomenon of 'light waves' refers to the patterns of light and shadow that can be observed when sunlight passes through the Earth's atmosphere. These patterns can provide valuable information about the composition and behavior of the Earth's atmosphere. The 2024 solar eclipse was particularly well-suited for this type of observation because of its path across the United States, which allowed scientists in Missouri to observe the event under optimal conditions.

author: Katie Hunt
title: Meteorites may be lost to Antarctic ice as climate warms, study says - CNN
mainText: Climate change poses a significant threat to the preservation of meteorites in Antarctica. A team of researchers from Switzerland and Belgium has calculated that for every tenth of a degree of increase in global air temperature, an average of nearly 9,000 meteorites disappear from the surface of the ice sheet. This loss has major implications, as meteorites are unique samples of extraterrestrial bodies that provide insights into the origin of life on Earth and the formation of the moon. By 2050, about a quarter of the estimated 300,000—800,000 meteorites in Antarctica will be lost due to glacial melt. By the end of the century, researchers anticipate that number could rise approaching a loss of meteorites closer to three-quarters of the meteorites on the continent under a high-warming scenario. The ongoing warming results in the loss of about 5,000 meteorites a year, outpacing the collection efforts of Antarctic meteorites by a factor of five. Meteorites are time capsules of the universe and once they disappear, so do some of the secrets of the universe.

author: Ed Cara
title: Scientists Discover How Bitter Taste Reception Actually Works - Gizmodo
mainText: Scientists have made a breakthrough in understanding how our mouths can taste bitterness. A recent study has revealed the structure of a key bitter taste receptor and has found evidence that cholesterol plays a significant role in enabling this receptor to function. Bitterness is one of the five basic tastes that humans can detect, along with sour, sweet, salty, and umami (a meaty, savory taste). It was already known that our sense of bitter taste is largely managed by certain receptors found in our tongue and mouth known as type 2 taste receptors, or TAS2Rs. Of these receptors, TAS2R14 is especially important, being able to identify over 100 substances that confer bitter taste. The new research was led by scientists from the University of North Carolina School of Medicine, who decided to take a much closer look at TAS2R14 than anyone has before. Their findings were published in the journal Nature. The researchers found cholesterol inside a binding site of the TAS2R14 receptor. This site was found next to another site meant to be activated by a specific bitter taste-inducing substance. The researchers suspect that cholesterol primes TAS2R14 so that it can be easily activated by this substance, though it might have other functions as well. While the team’s work has helped scientists get closer to understanding a crucial aspect of our sense of taste, it also sets the stage for future research. Based on their findings, it’s possible that TAS2R14 might have other functions besides simply helping us taste bitter food.

author: Mike Wall
title: Could these big expandable habitats help humanity settle the moon and Mars? - Space.com
mainText: Max Space, a pioneering startup, is aiming to propel humanity into the vast reaches of space with its innovative inflatable habitats. Unveiled at the 39th Space Symposium, these expandable structures offer the potential to revolutionize space habitation and pave the way for settlements on the moon and Mars. The startup is developing a range of inflatable space habitats, the largest of which could provide as much internal volume as a sports stadium. These plans are designed to help our species make the difficult leap off its home planet. Max Space co-founder Aaron Kemmer stated that unless we make usable space in space a lot less expensive, and much larger, humanity's future in space will remain limited. Expandable habitats, as the name suggests, launch in compressed form to fit inside rocket fairings but increase in size greatly when deployed in space. They therefore offer much more bang for the buck volume-wise than traditional module designs. An expandable habitat with 100 cubic meters of pressurized volume, for example, would be at least an order of magnitude cheaper than a comparable metallic one. This is not a sci-fi concept; three expandable module prototypes are actually circling Earth right now. They are Genesis 1 and Genesis 2, which are free fliers that launched in 2006 and 2007 respectively, and the Bigelow Expandable Activity Module (BEAM), which has been attached to the ISS since 2016.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: NASA's Mars helicopter Ingenuity finds 'otherworldly' wreckage on surface of Red Planet - UNILAD
mainText: NASA's Mars helicopter, Ingenuity, has made an intriguing discovery on the Martian surface. The helicopter, which has been operational since July 2020, has completed 72 flights over Mars as part of the Mars 2020 mission, far exceeding its initial goal of five flights. During one of its flights in 2022, Ingenuity came across a strange sight - a mysterious wreckage scattered across the Martian surface. However, this wreckage is not alien in origin. Instead, it is the debris from the landing equipment used when Ingenuity and the Perseverance rover arrived on Mars in 2021. The images captured by Ingenuity provide a unique perspective on the landing process and could be invaluable for future missions. Ian Clark, an engineer who worked on Perseverance’s parachute system, commented on the images, stating that they offer an 'infinite amount of engineering understanding.' Despite the mess we've made on Mars, these images could be particularly useful for technicians planning future missions. Teddy Tzanetos, Ingenuity's team lead at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, stated that every flight Ingenuity undertakes offers a perspective no previous planetary mission could achieve. Ingenuity's flights over Mars are hoped to help pave the way for future aerial explorers at Mars and potentially even other space destinations.

author: Harry Baker
title: No, you didn't see a solar flare during the total eclipse — but you may have seen something just as special - Livescience.com
mainText: Several media outlets have incorrectly claimed that explosive solar flares were spotted during the April 8 total solar eclipse. But there were no flares during totality, so what did people see? During the recent total solar eclipse, observers may have glimpsed what looked like explosive solar flares bursting from the sun after its fiery corona briefly came into view. But this was not the case. What was seen was equally impressive and just as beautiful. On Monday (April 8), millions of people across North America watched as the moon temporarily blocked out our home star and its shadow raced along the path of totality between Mexico and Canada at more than 1,500 mph (2,400 km/h). The cosmic event, which was also seen from space, was particularly special because of the length of totality — the period when the sun's light was completely obscured — which lasted for up to 4 minutes and 28 seconds. During totality, some observers saw red dots around the obscured sun. Detailed photos of these dots revealed they were actually plasma, including a particularly large, fiery plume on the sun's southwest limb. As a result, multiple outlets including USA Today and NDTV reported that these fiery structures were produced by solar flares — explosions on the sun's surface that can launch massive clouds of plasma, known as coronal mass ejections (CMEs), into space. Lots of observers also took to social media to share their photos of these "solar flares." But experts weighed in to point out there were no solar flares during the eclipse. "There are many (incorrectly) reporting that a solar flare was visible during the total solar eclipse," Ryan French, an astrophysicist at the National Solar Observatory in Colorado, wrote on the social platform X. "This is sadly untrue, and the bright feature seen by millions was actually a prominence. These are longer-lived plasma structures, and not explosive like flares." Solar activity data backs up French's claim. On April 8, there was just one minor C-class solar flare that ended several hours before totality began anywhere in the U.S., and it did not launch a CME, according to SpaceWeatherLive.com.

author: Neuroscience News
title: Bridging Brain Circuits with Lab-Grown Neural Networks - Neuroscience News
mainText: Researchers have made significant strides in connecting lab-grown brain tissues, thereby simulating the intricate networks found in the human brain. This innovative method involves linking 'neural organoids' with axonal bundles, which allows for the study of interregional brain connections and their role in human cognitive functions. The connected organoids displayed more sophisticated activity patterns, demonstrating both the generation and synchronization of electrical activity similar to natural brain functions. This breakthrough not only enhances our understanding of brain network development and plasticity but also opens new avenues for researching neurological and psychiatric disorders, offering hope for more effective treatments. The research team linked neural organoids using axonal bundles, achieving more physiologically accurate connections that mirror those in the human brain. This connection method allowed for the observation of complex activity patterns and plasticity in the organoids, showing promise for studying brain functions and disorders. The study represents a significant step forward in creating functional brain-like tissues in the lab, providing a powerful tool for understanding human brain networks and their implications in health and disease. The idea of growing a functioning human brain-like tissues in a dish has always sounded pretty far-fetched, even to researchers in the field. Towards the future goal, a Japanese and French research team has developed a technique for connecting lab-grown brain-mimicking tissue in a way that resembles circuits in our brain. It is challenging to study the exact mechanisms of brain development and functions. Animal studies are limited by differences between species in brain structure and function, and brain cells grown in the lab tend to lack the characteristic connections of cells in the human brain. Researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, find that providing lab-grown ‘cerebral organoids’ with connections similar to those in real brains enhances their development and activity. What’s more, researchers are increasingly realizing that these interregional connections, and the circuits that they create, are important for many of the brain functions that define us as humans. Previous studies have tried to create brain circuits under laboratory conditions, which have been advancing the field. Researchers from The University of Tokyo have recently found a way to create more physiological connections between lab-grown 'neural organoids,' an experimental model tissue in which human stem cells are grown into three-dimensional developmental brain-mimicking structures. The team did this by linking the organoids via axonal bundles, which is similar to how regions are connected in the living human brain.

title: NASA, Japan Advance Space Cooperation, Sign Agreement for Lunar Rover - NASA
mainText: NASA Administrator Bill Nelson and Japan's Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) Masahito Moriyama have signed an agreement to advance sustainable human exploration of the Moon. Under this agreement, Japan will design, develop, and operate a pressurized rover for crewed and uncrewed exploration on the Moon. NASA will provide the launch and delivery of the rover to the Moon as well as two opportunities for Japanese astronauts to travel to the lunar surface. The signing took place on April 9, 2024, at the NASA Headquarters Mary W. Jackson Building in Washington. President Biden and Prime Minister Kishida also announced a shared goal for a Japanese national to be the first non-American astronaut to land on the Moon on a future Artemis mission, assuming important benchmarks are achieved. The pressurized lunar rover is intended to enable astronauts to travel farther and work for longer periods on the lunar surface. An enclosed and pressurized rover will enable astronauts to travel farther and conduct science in geographically diverse areas by serving as a mobile habitat and laboratory for the astronauts to live and work for extended periods of time. It will be able to accommodate two astronauts for up to 30 days as they traverse the area near the lunar South Pole. NASA currently plans to use the pressurized rover on Artemis VII and subsequent missions over an approximate 10-year lifespan. The quest for the stars is led by nations that explore the cosmos openly, in peace, and together. This is true for the United States and Japan under the leadership of President Biden and Prime Minister Kishida. America no longer will walk on the Moon alone. With this new rover, we will uncover groundbreaking discoveries on the lunar surface that will benefit humanity and inspire the Artemis Generation.

mainText: Akebono Taro, a sumo wrestling legend who also competed in WWE's WrestleMania 21, has passed away at the age of 54. Born in Hawaii, Akebono was the first foreign-born sumo star to reach the level of 'yokozuna', or grand champion. His family announced his death earlier this month, stating that he died of heart failure while receiving care at a hospital in the Tokyo area. Akebono, whose real name was Chad George Ha'aheo Rowan, was raised in Honolulu near the Koolau mountains. He moved to Tokyo in the 1980s and by 1993, he had won a grand championship and become a 'yokozuna'. He was an 11-time tournament winner and retired from sumo in 2001. Akebono also brought his skills to WWE in 2005 when he defeated Big Show at WrestleMania 21 in a Los Angeles exhibition match by throwing him out of the ring. At the height of his career, he weighed over 500 pounds and stood at 6 feet, 8 inches. His career spanned across sports and continents, and his success opened the door for other foreign wrestlers in the sport. His passing was mourned by many, including his great rival in the sumo world, grand champion Wakanohana (real name Masaru Hanada).
