author: ANI
title: Childhood maltreatment continues to impact mental, physical health in adulthood: Study - Hindustan Times
mainText: Childhood abuse and neglect can have a greater impact on mental health later in life depending on how it is remembered and processed, according to research. The way childhood abuse and/or neglect is remembered and processed has a greater impact on later mental health than the experience itself, according to new research from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology, and Neuroscience (IoPPN) at King’s College London and City University New York, published today (Wednesday 5 July) in JAMA Psychiatry. Even in the lack of documented evidence, the authors argue that physicians can use patients’ self-reported experiences of abuse and neglect to identify those at risk of developing mental health problems and provide early interventions. The way childhood abuse and/or neglect is remembered and processed has a greater impact on later mental health than the experience itself. Researchers conducted a large longitudinal study following 1,196 participants to age 40 years to investigate how experiences of childhood abuse and/or neglect (maltreatment) impact the development of emotional disorders in adulthood. The study found that young adults who retrospectively self-reported experiences of childhood maltreatment before age 12 had a greater number of depressive or anxiety episodes over the subsequent decade than those who did not remember maltreatment, even if they had an official court record. In contrast, participants who had an official record of childhood maltreatment, but no retrospective recall of the experience, had a similar number of emotional disorder episodes in adulthood as those with no experience of maltreatment. Andrea Danese, Professor of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry at King’s IoPPN and joint author of the study, said: 'Our study reveals that how a person perceives and remembers experiences of childhood abuse or neglect has greater implications on future emotional disorders than the experience itself. The findings show that, even in the absence of documented evidence of childhood maltreatment, clinicians can use information provided by their clients to identify those at greater risk for subsequent mental health difficulties. The findings also suggest that early interventions that help cope with memories of abuse and/or neglect may prevent emotional problems later on.' Participants were interviewed about their self-reported retrospective experiences of childhood maltreatment and their current and past mental health. They were then re-interviewed to measure the course of depression and anxiety symptoms. Further analyses revealed that the association between self-reported experiences of childhood maltreatment and a greater number of subsequent anxiety and depression episodes was partly explained by participants’ current and past mental health, which was reported during their first interview.

author: Lifestyle Desk
title: From tea to rice: 5 food items you should never reheat (and why) - The Indian Express
mainText:
When it comes to reheating food, some items are best left untouched. Whether it’s for safety reasons or maintaining the taste and texture, certain foods don’t fare well when reheated. Here are five food items you should avoid reheating:

1. Tea: Reheating tea can alter its flavor and make it bitter. The tannins in tea react with oxygen, leading to a change in taste. It’s best to brew fresh tea when needed.
2. Rice: Reheating cooked rice can be risky due to the potential growth of harmful bacteria. Rice contains spores of Bacillus cereus, which can multiply during storage and cause food poisoning. If you have leftover rice, refrigerate it promptly and consume it within a day.
3. Potatoes: Reheating potatoes can lead to the formation of toxic compounds. When cooked and cooled, potatoes develop resistant starches. Reheating breaks down these starches into simple sugars, which can form acrylamide—a potentially harmful substance. It’s safer to eat potatoes fresh or cold.
4. Eggs: Reheating eggs can result in an unpleasant texture and odor. Eggs contain proteins that denature upon reheating, leading to rubbery or grainy consistency. If you have leftover eggs, consume them cold or use them in dishes that don’t require reheating.
5. Spinach: Reheating spinach can cause the conversion of nitrates into nitrites, which are potentially harmful. Nitrites can interfere with hemoglobin’s ability to transport oxygen in the blood. If you’ve cooked spinach, consume it immediately or store it in the refrigerator without reheating.

Remember to handle leftovers carefully and follow proper food safety guidelines to avoid any health risks.

author: Republic Lifestyle Desk
title: Fairness Creams Leading To Kidney Issues? New Study Suggests Correlation - Republic World
mainText: A new study has revealed a concerning correlation between the use of fairness creams and the rise in kidney issues in India. The study, published in the medical journal Kidney International, indicates that the high levels of mercury found in these creams can lead to a condition known as Membranous Nephropathy (MN). MN damages the kidney filters, resulting in protein leakage. This condition is an autoimmune disease that results in a kidney disorder known as nephrotic syndrome, which causes the body to excrete too much protein in the urine. The study examined 22 cases of MN reported between July 2021 and September 2023. The patients presented with symptoms that were often subtle, including fatigue, mild edema, and increased frothing of urine. Only three patients had gross edema, but all had elevated protein levels in their urine. One patient developed cerebral vein thrombosis, a blood clot in the brain, but renal function was preserved in all. The findings showed that about 68 per cent or 15 out of the 22 were positive for neural epidermal growth factor-like 1 protein (NELL-1) a rare form of MN that is more likely to be associated with malignancy. Of the 15 patients, 13 admitted using skin fairness creams before their symptom onset. Of the rest, one had a history of use of traditional indigenous medicines while the other had no identifiable trigger. Most cases resolved on cessation of use of the inciting creams. This poses a potential public health risk, and it is imperative to spread public awareness about hazards of using such products and alert health authorities to curb this menace.

author: Clare Watson
title: Massive Study Links Vaping to a Much Higher Risk of Heart Failure - ScienceAlert
mainText: In 2019, a health crisis emerged in the United States. Over 2,800 individuals were hospitalized and 68 people lost their lives due to a common probable cause – a chemical present in certain vaping products that damages lung tissue, leading to severe respiratory distress. This alarming event triggered extensive research into the potential health risks associated with vaping. Five years on, substantial evidence from comprehensive, long-term studies has consistently indicated that e-cigarette usage is associated with an elevated risk of respiratory diseases, heart attacks, and strokes. A recent study presented at the annual scientific meeting of the American College of Cardiology further substantiates these findings. The study revealed that individuals aged 18 and above who have used e-cigarettes at any point in their lives are 19 percent more likely to suffer from heart failure compared to those who have never used them. Heart failure, unlike a sudden heart attack, is a gradual process where the heart weakens or stiffens to the point where it struggles to pump blood efficiently throughout the body. Yakubu Bene-Alhasan, a physician and researcher at MedStar Health in Baltimore, expressed concern over the growing body of evidence suggesting that e-cigarettes may not be as safe as previously believed. The study, which is the largest of its kind to explore the association between e-cigarette usage and heart failure, has not yet undergone peer review. Bene-Alhasan and his team analyzed the health records of 175,667 US adults participating in the US National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program. Out of these participants, 28,660 reported having used e-cigarettes at some point, and 3,242 experienced heart failure during the nearly four years of median follow-up data collected. The researchers adjusted for factors such as age, sex, and other conditions linked to heart failure, including diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and smoking status. The study found that compared to those who had never vaped, former and current e-cigarette users had a 19 percent increased risk of heart failure, specifically a type where the heart muscle stiffens and doesn't fill with blood properly.

author: RealClearPolitics
title: U.S. Fatalities in 2023 Return to Pre-Pandemic Trendline - RealClearPolitics
mainText: The number of fatalities in the United States in 2023 declined to 3,078,290 from 3,269,042 in 2022, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. This figure aligns closely with the pre-pandemic trendline. From 1960-2019, the U.S. fatality rate (fatalities per 1,000 population) was approximately 8.75, with a range from a high of 9.5 to a low of 7.9. From 1970-2010, there was a slight downtrend in the rate. However, starting in 2011, the rate began a slow but steady increase, associated with an aging population and a slight decline in life expectancy. The fatality rate saw a significant jump during the pandemic. For 2020-2022, the rate averaged 10.2, about a 22% increase from before the pandemic. The rate for 2023 was 9.1. In the 10 years prior to the pandemic, the increase in rate was running at about 1.3% per year. If there had been no pandemic and that trend would have continued, the rate last year would have been almost exactly 9.1. It is estimated that during 2020-2022, around 1.4 million more people died than we would have expected had there been no pandemic. The CDC estimates that about 1.2 million died from COVID. There was an increase in fatalities that exceeded the number the disease caused. Many of these fatalities were likely caused by unintended consequences of our reaction to the virus. Drug overdoses increased during the pandemic and certain chronic drivers of fatalities, like cardiovascular issues and cancer, were up due to a decline in routine early detection. In less developed countries, collateral fatalities were almost certainly even higher. The coronavirus pandemic exacted an enormous toll on our country and the entire world, and not just in the additional fatalities it caused. Much of the damage was attributable to the lethality and the transmissibility of the disease. But a great deal of the damage was also due to our reactions to it.

author: Iti Dewangan, Iti Dewangan
title: India Now The 'Cancer Capital Of The World' Says A Recent Report - Feminism In India
mainText: India, often celebrated for its cultural heritage and traditions, faces a grim reality as it gains the unfortunate title of “Cancer Capital of the world.” A recent report by Apollo Hospitals declared India as a “Cancer Capital.” This alarming title reflects statistics and reports highlighting the increasing prevalence of cancer cases across the nation. However, its impact on women makes this situation even more poignant. Over the last ten years, women’s cancer cases in India have increased significantly. This worrying trend is influenced by several factors, including changing lifestyles, pollution in the environment, genetic predispositions, and a lack of knowledge. Among the most common cancers afflicting Indian women are breast, cervical, ovarian, and uterine cancers. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), cancer progresses from a precancerous condition to malignancy, usually through a multi-stage process in which normal cells undergo a transition into tumour cells. These changes result from the interaction between a person’s genetic composition and three primary categories of extrinsic factors: physical carcinogens, such as radiation from ionising and ultraviolet light. Chemical carcinogens include drinking water contaminated with arsenic, aflatoxin (a food contaminant), alcohol, tobacco smoke, and asbestos. Biological carcinogens include infections brought on by certain bacteria, viruses, or parasites. Air pollution, bad food, alcohol use, smoking, and physical inactivity are risk factors for noncommunicable diseases including cancer. Certain chronic infections increase the risk of cancer; this is especially problematic in low- and middle-income nations. Carcinogenic diseases, such as Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Epstein-Barr virus (2), were linked to almost 13 per cent of malignancies reported worldwide in 2018. The risk of liver and cervical cancer is elevated by the hepatitis B and C viruses and certain forms of HPV, respectively. HIV infection significantly raises the risk of some other malignancies, such as Kaposi sarcoma, and increases the chance of cervical cancer by a factor of six.

mainText: Researchers at UCL have invented innovative carbon beads that reduce bad bacteria and inflammation in animal models, which are linked to liver cirrhosis and other serious health issues. The study, published in Gut, found that the carbon beads, licensed to UCL-spinout Yaqrit, were effective in restoring gut health and had a positive impact on liver, kidney and brain function in rats and mice. They were also found to be safe for human use. The next step will be to see if the same benefits can be realized in humans, which would pave the way for them to be used to treat diseases linked to poor gut health. Worldwide, it is estimated that there are around 100 million people living with cirrhosis of the liver and 10 million who have cirrhosis plus an additional complication. The influence of the gut microbiome on health is only just beginning to be fully appreciated. When the balance of the microbiome is upset, 'bad' bacteria can proliferate and out-compete the 'good' bacteria that keeps the gut healthy. One of the ways they do this is by excreting endotoxin, toxic metabolites and cytokines that transform the gut environment to make it more favorable to them and hostile to good bacteria. These substances, particularly endotoxin, can trigger gut inflammation and increase the leakiness of the gut wall, resulting in damage to other organs such as the liver, kidneys and brain. In cirrhosis, a condition characterized by scarring of the liver, it is known that inflammation caused by endotoxins can exacerbate liver damage. Part of the standard treatment for cirrhosis is antibiotics aimed at controlling bad bacteria, but this comes with the risk of antibiotic resistance and is only used in late-stage disease. To overcome this, scientists at UCL, in collaboration with Yaqrit, developed tiny oral carbon beads, that have a special microscopic physical structure designed to adsorb both large and small molecules in the gut. In the study, researchers from UCL tested the effectiveness of the carbon beads, known by the product name CARBALIVE, to restore gut health and assessed the impact on liver, kidney and brain function in rats and mice. They found that when ingested every day for several weeks, the beads were effective in preventing the progress of liver scarring and injury in animals with cirrhosis, and reduced mortality in animals with acute-on-chronic-liver-failure (ACLF). The beads were also tested on 28 cirrhosis patients and proved to be safe with negligible side effects.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: CDC: No link between COVID vaccine and cardiac deaths in young people - WRAL News
mainText: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has found no link between the COVID-19 vaccines and cardiac deaths in young people. This conclusion is based on an analysis of death certificates from Oregon residents who died from any heart condition or unknown reasons between June 2020 and 2021 and December 2020 and 2022. The study reviewed over 1,300 death certificates of people between 16 years old and 30 years old. Out of the 101 death certificates where a cardiac event wasn’t ruled out as a cause of death, 40 people received the vaccination, and only three of those people received the vaccine within 100 days of their death. The study was conducted in response to claims that young people experience inflammation of the heart muscle after receiving the vaccine. The findings of the study show that the data do not support an association of COVID-19 vaccination with sudden cardiac death among previously healthy young persons. This study is significant as it debunks widespread misinformation that the mRNA shots were connected to sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

author: Tracy Swartz
title: Diet Coke or Coke Zero? Dietitian reveals which one is healthier - New York Post
mainText: A Toronto-based registered dietitian, Abbey Sharp, has evaluated the healthfulness of the no-calorie diet sodas Coke Zero and Diet Coke. Both contain aspartame, caffeine, natural flavors, and caramel colors. The key difference is that Diet Coke is sweetened exclusively with aspartame, whereas Coke Zero also contains a sweetener called acesulfame potassium or Ace-K. While some wellness communities call both of these sweeteners complete poison, they’re both FDA-approved and have been deemed safe in moderation. Aspartame, sold under the brand names Nutrasweet, Equal, and Sugar Twin, is about 200 times sweeter than sugar. Last year, the World Health Organization’s cancer research arm classified aspartame as “possibly carcinogenic to humans,” calling for further research on potential health risks. However, the Food and Drug Administration disagreed with that label, noting that it “does not mean that aspartame is actually linked to cancer.” The FDA says the acceptable daily intake for aspartame is up to 50 milligrams per kilogram of body weight each day. Ace-K, also known as Sunett and Sweet One, is also about 200 times sweeter than table sugar. The FDA regulates Ace-K as a food additive, emphasizing that it has reviewed more than 90 studies of possible toxic effects of the substance. A 2022 French study linked aspartame to an increased risk of stroke and Ace-K to a higher risk of coronary artery disease. Sharp said, “I’m generally not concerned about either of these sweeteners, though I prefer not to take the risk specifically in pregnancy with Ace-K because it has been shown to cross the placenta.” Another major difference between Diet Coke and Coke Zero, Sharp points out, is caffeine content. A 12-ounce can of Diet Coke has about 46 milligrams, while Coke Zero has 34 milligrams. In drawing her conclusion, Sharp said discipline is key. “Honestly, diet sodas are not health foods. They should be treated no differently than regular, full-sugar soda,” she reasoned.

author: sahas, Buzz Staff
title: When The Brightest-ever Supernova Yielded No Trace Of Gold Or Platinum In 2022 - News18
mainText: The recent burst of light, dubbed GRB 221009A, occurred an astounding two billion light years away. On October 9, 2022, an extraordinary surge of intense radiation was observed throughout the solar system. Gold and platinum are considered some of the rarest and most valuable metals on Earth. For years, scientists believed that these precious metals were formed during massive solar explosions called supernovae. However, a recent discovery challenges this long-held belief. In 2022, astronomers observed an extraordinary event in space. On October 9th of that year, there was a massive burst of intense radiation that lit up the solar system like never before. This event, nicknamed BOAT, was identified as a gamma-ray burst (GRB), the most powerful type of explosion known to scientists. Despite its incredible brightness, when scientists examined the data collected from the event, they were surprised to find no traces of gold or platinum, which are typically associated with supernovae. This finding contradicted their expectations. Dr Peter Blanchard, who led the study, explained that the absence of these heavy elements challenges existing theories about their formation. He noted that highly energetic GRBs like BOAT may not produce gold and platinum as previously thought. This discovery has sparked further investigation into cosmic processes to understand how these elements are formed. The exact cause of the supernova’s brightness remains uncertain. Some researchers speculate that the release of a powerful plasma jet may have contributed to its intensity. GRB 221009A, as it’s officially known, is considered the brightest burst of energy in X-ray and gamma-ray wavelengths. This unexpected discovery has significant implications for our understanding of the universe. It suggests that the formation of precious metals like gold and platinum may occur through different processes than previously thought. Scientists are now eager to explore these new avenues of research to uncover the mysteries of cosmic evolution. The discovery of the BOAT supernova, despite its immense brightness, revealed the absence of gold and platinum, challenging existing theories of their formation. This unexpected finding opens up new questions and avenues of research in astrophysics, pushing scientists to rethink our understanding of the cosmos.

author: INDIATODAYNE
title: Fascinating Facts About Human Bones - India Today NE
mainText:
Our bones are remarkable structures that provide support, protect vital organs, and allow movement. Here are some intriguing facts about human bones:

1. Adults Have 206 Bones: At birth, humans have around 270 bones, but as they grow, some bones fuse together. By adulthood, the typical human skeleton consists of 206 bones.

2. Longest Bone: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest bone in the human body. It plays a crucial role in walking, running, and supporting body weight.

3. Smallest Bone: The stapes bone in the middle ear is the smallest bone. It measures just a few millimeters and is involved in transmitting sound vibrations.

4. Bone Regeneration: Our bones constantly undergo remodeling. Old bone tissue is broken down by osteoclasts, while osteoblasts build new bone tissue.

5. Bone Marrow: Bone marrow, found inside bones, produces blood cells. Red bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

6. Bone Density: Peak bone density occurs around age 30. After that, bone density gradually decreases, leading to conditions like osteoporosis.

7. Collagen and Minerals: Bones are composed of collagen fibers and minerals like calcium and phosphorus. Collagen provides flexibility, while minerals give strength.

8. Ribs Protect Organs: The rib cage protects vital organs like the heart and lungs. It also assists in breathing by expanding and contracting.

9. Skull Bones: The human skull consists of 22 bones, including the cranial bones that encase the brain and the facial bones.

10. Hyoid Bone: The hyoid bone, located in the neck, doesn’t directly connect to other bones. It supports the tongue and aids in swallowing.

Understanding these fascinating aspects of our skeletal system highlights the intricate design and functionality of our bones.

author: iednewsdesk
title: Mediterranean Marine Worm Develops Eyes 'as Big as Millstones', Study Reveals - India Education Diary
mainText: The Vanadis bristle worm, a Mediterranean marine worm, has developed eyes that are as big as millstones, relatively speaking. If our eyes were proportionally as big as the ones of this worm, we would need a big sturdy wheelbarrow and brawny arms to lug around the extra 100kg. The worm’s eyes weigh about twenty times as much as the rest of the animal’s head and seem grotesquely out of place on this tiny and transparent marine critter. It appears as if two giant, shiny red balloons have been strapped to its body. The Vanadis worm belongs to a family of large-eyed bristle worms, or polychaeta, found in many parts of the world. Its eyesight rivals that of rodents such as mice and rats. The worms can see UV light and focus on relatively small objects, tracking them as they move. It is nocturnal. The researchers believe that these bristle worms use their eyes to communicate for mating and hunting prey. Vanadis bristle worms, also known as polychaetes, can be found around the Italian island of Ponza, just west of Naples. Like some of the island’s summertime partiers, the worms are nocturnal and out of sight when the sun is high in the sky. Neuro- and marine biologist Anders Garm from the University of Copenhagen’s Department of Biology couldn’t ignore the question. Setting other plans aside, the researcher felt compelled to dive in and try to find out. He was hooked as soon as his colleague Michael Bok at Lund University showed him a recording of the bristle worm. Together, they set out to unravel the mystery of why a nearly invisible, transparent worm that feeds in the dead of night has evolved to acquire enormous eyes. As such, the first aim was to answer whether large eyes endow the worm with good vision. It turns out that the Vanadis’ eyesight is excellent and advanced. Research has demonstrated that this worm can use its eyes to see small objects and track their movements. This ability is typically reserved for us vertebrates, along with arthropods (insects, spiders, etc.) and cephalopods (octopus, squid). This is the first time that such an advanced and detailed view has been demonstrated beyond these groups. In fact, the research has shown that the worm has outstanding vision. Its eyesight is on a par with that of mice or rats, despite being a relatively simple organism with a miniscule brain.

author: iednewsdesk
title: PolyU Researchers Introduce Biomineralisation to Combat Microbial Corrosion in Marine Concrete - India Education Diary
mainText: Microbially induced corrosion (MIC) is a significant problem in marine environments, causing structural damages such as cracking in concrete infrastructure. This corrosion is a persistent challenge, significantly reducing the lifespan of marine structures and leading to substantial economic losses. To address the need for an effective solution to combat marine corrosion on concrete, researchers from The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) have developed a biomineralisation approach to protect marine concrete from MIC. Prof. Xiang-dong LI, Dean of the Faculty of Construction and Environment, Director of the Research Institute for Sustainable Urban Development, Chair Professor of Environmental Science and Technology, and Ko Jan Ming Professor in Sustainable Urban Development at PolyU, has spearheaded the research that successfully introduces a novel biomineralisation strategy. This strategy effectively isolates marine concrete from MIC, thereby contributing to the achievement of sustainable coastal structures. MIC on concrete typically occurs in harsh environments with the presence of corrosive microorganisms, such as in sewage structures, wastewater treatment plants, and marine structures. The formation of a biomineralised film on concrete surfaces is generally considered to be the major anticorrosion mechanism as it can provide a barrier to inhibit corrosion. Prof. LI said, 'Our biomineralisation technique serves as an environmentally friendly coating method for controlling concrete corrosion, with minimal impact on the overall biofilm communities. Also, it utilises carbon dioxide to produce mineral precipitates, enhancing the durability of concrete structures. This process not only reduces the carbon footprint and energy consumption of marine infrastructure throughout its lifespan, but also makes a valuable contribution to carbon neutrality and sustainability.' The study showed that the biomineralisation treatment effectively prevents corrosion by reducing the total and relative abundance of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB). SRB is a type of anaerobic bacteria and can produce hydrogen sulfide, which is corrosive and can lead to material deterioration. The biomineralised film acts as a protective layer, controlling sulfate diffusion and isolating the concrete from the corrosive SRB communities. This protective mechanism significantly extends the lifespan of concrete structures. Moreover, this technique has no negative impact on the native marine microbial communities. Prof. LI added, 'If the biomineralised film remains intact, repainting the concrete structures is unnecessary. The utilisation of a single coating treatment eliminates the need for multiple treatments, further minimising the cost and carbon footprint.'

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: NASA set to make massive announcement about Mars Sample Return mission. Check date and time - WION
mainText: NASA is set to make a significant announcement about its Mars Sample Return mission. The announcement will be made during a media teleconference on April 15, 2024, at 01:00 pm EDT (10:30 pm IST in India). The Mars Sample Return mission has been in a challenging situation, and NASA will outline its recommendations for moving forward during the teleconference. The Perseverance rover, which was deployed in 2021, is a part of this mission. The rover's objective was to collect fascinating samples of Martian rock gathered by another mission and return them to Earth. However, an independent review last year stated that the Mars Sample Return (MSR) had an 'unrealistic budget and schedule,' an 'unwieldy structure,' and was 'not arranged to be led effectively.' This review put the future of the MSR mission in jeopardy. Following the review, the House and Senate appropriations committees proposed a budget that included a cut of $454,080,000 to NASA's 2024 budget. The Mars Sample Return Mission was severely affected by this cut. Furthermore, NASA has reduced its overall expenditure on the mission and has laid off several workers and contractors from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is leading the mission. There have been concerns that NASA might abandon the mission and the canisters loaded by Perseverance might be left useless on the Martian surface due to the budget cuts and layoffs. However, NASA's upcoming announcement provides a ray of hope for the mission. NASA states, 'Mars Sample Return has been a major long-term goal of international planetary exploration for the past two decades. NASA's Perseverance rover is collecting compelling science samples that will help scientists understand the geological history of Mars, the evolution of its climate and prepare for future human explorers. The return of the samples will also help NASA's search for signs of ancient life.' According to the current plan, an orbiter will launch in 2027, a lander will launch in 2028, and unique Mars samples will return to Earth in 2033.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Giant kangaroo, double the size of animals we know today once `hopped` across Australia: Study - WION
mainText: Giant kangaroos, which were double the weight of the kangaroos we know today, once hopped across Australia. These creatures have become a mystery that scientists are still trying to unravel. Until now, our knowledge about them was limited due to the isolated bones making it difficult to distinguish species. However, recent research has identified three now-extinct giant marsupial species. According to a team of Paleontologists from Flinders University, these three species — Protemnodon viator, Protemnodon mamkurra, and Protemnodon dawsonae — lived around 5 million to 40,000 years ago. The extinct genus Protemnodon resembled today's grey kangaroo but was generally more squat and muscular. Some species were only around 45-50 kg, while others were much larger than any living kangaroo. Of the three recently identified species, Protemnodon viator weighed around 170kg, double the weight of the heaviest present-day red males, which can weigh up to 90 kg. Viator, which means 'traveller' or 'wayfarer' in Latin, were long-limbed kangaroos that could hop fairly quickly and efficiently. The research team suggests that the giant kangaroo lived in similar areas as the red kangaroos of today and was well-adapted to the arid central Australian habitat. The other two species — Protemnodon mamkurra and Protemnodon dawsonae — are new. The newly described Protemnodon mamkurra is likely one of these. A large but thick-boned and robust kangaroo, it was probably fairly slow-moving and inefficient. It may have hopped only rarely, perhaps just when startled. Earlier, experts believed that these Protemnodon moved on all four legs. However, the research led by Isaac Kerr suggests that this was only true for about three or four species. Others, they believe, moved like a quokka or potoroo, bounding on four legs at times, and hopping on two legs at others. The research follows the discovery of multiple complete fossilised Kangaroo skeletons from Lake Callabonna in arid South Australia in 2013, 2018, and 2019.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Mercury May Once Have Been As Large As Earth, Says Scientist - NDTV
mainText: Mercury, the smallest planet in the Solar System and the one closest to the Sun, is known for its extremes. A geologist from Italy, Nicola Mari, who is a planetary geologist at the University of Pavia, recently found clues in Cyprus that point towards a different origin story for Mercury. The planet experiences extreme temperature fluctuations due to its proximity to the Sun. Daytime temperatures can soar up to a blistering 800 degree Fahrenheit (427 degrees Celsius), while night-time temperatures plummet to a frigid -290 degrees Fahrenheit (-180 degrees Celsius). Orbiting the Sun at a breakneck pace, Mercury completes a full orbit in just 88 Earth days, making it the shortest year of any planet in our solar system. But studying the planet is very difficult due to its position and the impact of the Sun's gravity. This is why scientists have resorted to finding clues on Earth that could help them understand the composition of Mercury. During a recent visit to Cyprus, Mr Mari made an astonishing discovery - that Mercury was once as big as the Earth. In Cyprus, the geologist was looking for "boninite", a rock that is thought to bear an uncanny similarity to the rocks found on Mercury - a supposition which, if right, could be a clue to the planet's unique origins. Cyprus was formed under the Tethys Ocean more than 90 million years ago and was thrust towards the surface by colliding tectonic plates. He was astonished to find the similarity between the composition of rocks found on Mercury and boninites. "They weren't just similar; they were identical," said Mr Mari. The mix of elements such as magnesium, aluminium and iron was the same as that seen on the mysterious planet with the huge core. The only difference was that the rocks from Cyprus had been oxidised - which is inevitable given Earth's oxygen-rich atmosphere. Mr Mari said further study of these rocks might help reveal some clues about the geological activity in Mercury's past. The data led scientists to believe that Mercury was formed near to Mars - and that it started out with a much bigger mass, around the size of the Earth, that would befit its large core.

author: iednewsdesk
title: Scientists Unveil Potential Fate of Solar System in Groundbreaking White Dwarf Research - India Education Diary
mainText: Astrophysicists from the University of Warwick and other universities have made a groundbreaking discovery about the potential fate of our solar system. They suggest that our solar system might be pulled into the gravity of a white dwarf star, crushed and ground to dust. White dwarfs are the end state of stars when they have burned all their fuel, offering insight into different aspects of star formation and evolution. The researchers investigated the fate of asteroids, moons and planets which pass close to the white dwarfs, by analysing transits – which are dips in the brightness of stars caused by objects passing in front of them. Unlike the predictable transits caused by orbiting planets around stars, transits caused by debris are oddly shaped, chaotic and disorderly. This suggests the fate of these bodies to be extremely catastrophic and violent. Dr Amornrat Aungwerojwit of Naresuan University, who led the study, said: 'Previous research had shown that when asteroids, moons and planets get close to white dwarfs, the huge gravity of these stars rips these small planetary bodies into smaller and smaller pieces.' Collisions between these pieces eventually grind them into dust, which finally falls into the white dwarf, enabling researchers to determine what type of material the original planetary bodies were made from. In this new research, scientists investigated changes in brightness of stars for 17 years, shedding insight into how these bodies are disrupted. They focused on three different white dwarfs which all behaved very differently. Professor Boris Gaensicke, Department of Physics, University of Warwick, commented: 'The simple fact that we can detect the debris of asteroids, maybe moons or even planets whizzing around a white dwarf every couple of hours is quite mind-blowing, but our study shows that the behaviour of these systems can evolve rapidly, in a matter of a few years. While we think we are on the right path in our studies, the fate of these systems is far more complex than we could have ever imagined.'

author: iednewsdesk
title: Warwick Astronomer Receives £3 Million Grant to Revolutionize Sky Observations - India Education Diary
mainText: An astronomer from the University of Warwick has been awarded a grant of £3 million to develop a 'digital telescope'. This innovative telescope will be capable of producing a highly sensitive continuous movie of the night sky. The new telescope will be used to detect explosive astrophysical events in real time, such as explosions of stars and merging of black holes. It will also be able to detect satellites, asteroids and hazardous space debris in orbit around the Earth. A typical astronomical facility involves a telescope attached to a sophisticated mount, which moves to track the Earth’s rotation. This digital telescope, however, will include dozens of small stationary telescopes, each equipped with a state-of-the-art sensor. The stationary telescopes do not track the sky, so as the Earth rotates the stars drift through the fields of view of the telescopes. Computers can then be used to correct for the Earth’s rotation and produce highly sensitive images of the sky. More sophisticated computer algorithms can be used to detect objects moving in any direction with any speed. This will typically include satellites and space debris, but potentially also include solar system objects approaching the Earth, such as asteroids and comets. Professor Don Pollacco will lead the project which is funded by the European Research Council (ERC) in partnership with the University of Warwick (contributing an additional £600K). The prototype digital telescope will include data from 52 telescopes and will most likely be located in the Canary Islands near the University of Warwick’s other facilities on the island of La Palma. Professor Pollacco said: “ It is incredible that in this day and age we do not have such technology to pick up explosive space events in real-time. Instead, we rely on nightly and weekly surveys to find new objects and then observe them again with more powerful facilities. Unfortunately, most of the important physics can only be observed near the time of the initial explosion, so early detection is vital. “Typical objects we are looking to detect include Supernova, which are explosions of stars at the end of their lives, and the merging of black holes and neutron stars, known as Gravitation Wave merger systems. “The movie data can also be used to detect small pieces of space debris helping to alleviate the growing threat they pose to our satellites in near-Earth orbit. Knowing accurate orbits for debris and satellites allows us to record and remove them from the movie, hence giving a clearer astronomical view, as well as cataloguing the orbits of the debris itself. “If the Digital Telescope works as we expect then its contribution will be transformational to both the study of astrophysical explosions and the population of artificial objects in near space.

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Data frameworks need to go beyond risk and reward ... they need to be ethical too - Chris Skinner's blog
mainText: Chris Skinner, a well-known figure in the fintech space, recently wrote a blog post discussing the need for data frameworks to go beyond just risk and reward considerations. He argues that they also need to be ethical. Skinner points out that while the use of customer data can provide many benefits, such as improved marketing strategies and enhanced security measures, it also raises important ethical questions. For instance, who owns the data? Who has the right to access and use it? And under what circumstances is it acceptable to share or sell this data? Skinner suggests that these questions are often overlooked in the rush to exploit the potential of big data. However, he warns that failing to address these issues could lead to a backlash from customers and regulators alike. Skinner also highlights the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and open banking in this context. He notes that while these technologies can enable more effective use of data, they also increase the potential for misuse. Therefore, he argues, it is crucial to develop ethical guidelines for their use. Skinner concludes by calling for a more balanced approach to data management, one that takes into account not only the potential benefits but also the ethical implications.

author: HT Tech
title: NASA says ‘bridge-sized’ asteroid to pass Earth by a close margin: Check size, speed and more - HT Tech
mainText: NASA has revealed that a bridge-sized asteroid, designated as Asteroid 2013 NK4, is expected to pass Earth today, April 15. The Near-Earth Asteroid (NEA) is expected to make its closest approach to the planet at a speed of about 59363 kilometres per hour. Despite its close approach, it is not expected to impact the planet. The asteroid will pass by the planet at a distance of approximately 3.2 million kilometres. While these space rocks are millions or even billions of kilometres away from Earth, their orbits bring them close to Earth on some occasions.

author: sahas, Buzz Staff
title: Study Reveals Venus Leaks Carbon And Oxygen - News18
mainText: The novel coronavirus has witnessed a number of mutations in the past year. Baffling the experts, a new study revealed that a woman with advanced HIV carried the virus for 216 days. Published on Thursday, the case report also stated that the virus accumulated more than 30 mutations. The 36-year-old infected woman is a resident of South Africa. As per a report by the Hindustan Times, the mutations involved 13 to the spike proteins, which helps the virus escape the immune response, and 19 others, which could change its behaviour, as per the study. “While most people effectively clear Sars-CoV-2, there are several reports of prolonged infection in immunosuppressed individuals. We present a case of prolonged infection of greater than 6 months with the shedding of high titter SARS-CoV-2 in an individual with advanced HIV and antiretroviral treatment failure. Through whole-genome sequencing at multiple time-points, we demonstrate the early emergence of the E484K substitution associated with escape from neutralizing antibodies, followed by other escape mutations and the N501Y substitution found in most variants of concern,” an excerpt of the study said. This provides support to the hypothesis of intra-host evolution as one mechanism for the emergence of Sars-CoV-2 variants with immune evasion properties, it added. However, the experts are yet to find if the mutations that the woman was carrying were transmissible or not. A person carrying HIV is 2.75 times more likely to die when infected with the coronavirus than someone with no comorbidities. But in this case study, the woman was immunosuppressed. Reportedly, the impact of HIV had on mortality was less than expected and well below that of other co-morbidities such as diabetes. However, the risk is higher than tuberculosis, as per an analysis of the South African data done by the Western Cape Department of Health last year showed. About 7.8 million people in South Africa are infected with HIV, which causes AIDS, while about 300,000 have TB.

author: Anjali Marar
title: Space weather conspired with other factors in the unprecedented loss of 38 Starlink satellites: study - The Indian Express
mainText: Multiple factors, including poor space weather conditions, led to the loss of 38 of the 49 Starlink satellites launched by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in February 2022, a new study has found. In an era where the dependence on satellite-based services and operations is ever increasing, the loss of operational satellites could derail telecommunication, navigation and other vital operations on Earth, besides causing huge economic losses. Starlink is a network of satellites operating to facilitate uninterrupted internet services in remote and inaccessible areas on Earth. These are small satellites launched at regular intervals into the Low Earth Orbit (LEO). During the past two years, a team at the Centre of Excellence in Space Sciences India (CESSI) and the Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Kolkata, in collaboration with international scientists performed a detailed study to probe the possible contributors to the de-orbiting of Starlink satellites. These solar physicists pinned down the prevailing space weather conditions, before and during the Starlink launch, to be moderate thereby increasing the mystery around the satellite losses. Space weather is the environment around the Earth, other planets, and celestial objects in our galaxy which is largely controlled by the Sun’s activities. Space weather is affected by solar storms, coronal mass ejections and other ejectiles emerging from the Sun. Around the Starlink satellite launch scheduled on February 3, 2022, the physicists said, space conditions were moderately disturbed, but these disturbances persisted over days. Based on Coronal Mass Ejections (CME) data obtained from the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the NASA Wind spacecraft, it was found that three geomagnetic storms had emerged from the Sun in quick succession and disturbed the near-Earth space environment. Speaking to The Indian Express, Dibyendu Nandi, head, CESSI, said, “These were moderate-intensity geomagnetic storms but together they stirred up persistent currents around the near-Earth atmosphere. These currents heated the upper atmosphere of the Earth which expanded and resulted in higher densities at LEO.

author: Srishty Choudhury
title: Meet IIT-JEE topper Raghu Mahajan, who joined IIT-Delhi with AIR 1 but left after few months due to... - DNA India
mainText: Raghu Mahajan, the national topper in the 2006 IIT-JEE, has carved a unique path in pursuit of his intellectual passion. Initially enrolled in the computer science and engineering program at IIT-Delhi, Mahajan midway decided later to switch to physics and mathematics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in May 2008 as he was dissatisfied with the academic atmosphere at IIT-Delhi. Mahajan's academic journey took him to MIT, where he found the environment conducive to his passion for physics. His commitment to this field is evident through the six papers he has published in leading physics journals in the United States. Currently, Raghu Mahajan is a Postdoctoral Researcher at Stanford University. He was previously a Postdoctoral Researcher at Princeton University. Interestingly, Mahajan also contributed to the Aam Aadmi Party's manifesto for the 2015 Delhi Assembly Elections. Mahajan also believes that individuals entering IIT at the age of 17 or 18 may not know their true career preferences, and pursuing research should stem from genuine interest rather than societal expectations.

author: Zhao Lei
title: Relay satellite ready for lunar mission service - Asia News NetworkAsia News Network - asianews.network
mainText: China has successfully launched a relay satellite, Queqiao 2 or Magpie Bridge 2, to lunar orbit. This satellite is expected to provide communication service to missions operating on the Moon's far side. The Queqiao 2 satellite was launched atop a Long March 8 carrier rocket from the Wenchang Space Launch Center in Hainan province. After a flight of about 24 minutes, the satellite was released from the rocket and entered a lunar transfer trajectory. The solar wings and communication antennas of the satellite smoothly unfolded. After completing these maneuvers, the Queqiao 2 began its journey toward the moon. Over the next few days, the spacecraft is scheduled to carry out a series of maneuvers, such as a midcourse trajectory correction and a braking operation, before it enters an elliptical frozen orbit to become the second relay satellite above the moon. After its arrival in the predetermined orbital position, Queqiao 2 is set to conduct two-way communication tests with the Chang’e 4 probe, which is on the lunar surface, and Chang’e 6, which is waiting to be launched at the Wenchang center, to examine its performance. Queqiao 2 is primarily tasked with relaying signals and data during the Chang’e 6 robotic mission, which is scheduled to be launched by a Long March 5 heavy-lift rocket before July. In the long term, the satellite will also serve the Chang’e 7 and 8 missions. These will be the basis for an ambitious multinational plan known as the International Lunar Research Station, which is expected to be built in the 2030s.

author: Georgina Torbet
title: Hubble spots a bright galaxy peering out from behind a dark nebula - Digital Trends
mainText: A new image from the Hubble Space Telescope reveals a galaxy partially obscured by a massive dust cloud, known as a dark nebula. The galaxy, IC 4633, continues to emit a bright and beautiful light, visible in the main portion of the image. However, towards the bottom right, dark patches of dust can be seen, blocking the light from this part of the galaxy. The image was captured using Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) instrument, and also includes data from the DECam instrument on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. By combining data from the space-based Hubble and the ground-based DECam, astronomers are able to gain a better understanding of this galaxy, which is located 100 million light-years away, and the dark dust that partially obscures it. The subject of this image, the spiral galaxy IC 4633, is located 100 million light-years away from us in the constellation Apus. IC 4633 is a galaxy rich in star-forming activity and hosts an active galactic nucleus at its core. From our perspective, the galaxy is mostly tilted towards us, providing astronomers with a fairly good view of its billions of stars. This galaxy is bustling with activity, with vigorous star formation and a bright center known as an active galactic nucleus. Thanks to its orientation relative to Earth, we can see the elegant spiral shape of the galaxy. Spiral galaxies tend to be symmetrical, so the less bright area with fewer stars at the bottom right of the galaxy indicates that something is obscuring it. The cloud of dust blocking the view is part of a star-forming region called Chamaeleon, and it is much closer to us than the galaxy it blocks. At just 500 light-years away, the dark nebula is much closer to Earth than the galaxy. When viewed in the visible light portion of the spectrum, these dust clouds appear dark and featureless. For many years, astronomers regarded such cosmic dust as nothing more than an annoyance that interfered with their observations. However, in recent years, the importance of cosmic dust has become apparent, as it plays a key role in processes like star formation. Dust becomes even more interesting when viewed in the infrared wavelength, with instruments like those used on the James Webb Space Telescope. Instruments operating in the infrared can peer through layers of dust to see structures that would otherwise be hidden, such as concentric dust shells around stars or the swirls of dust in nearby galaxies.

author: Michelle Starr
title: The Most Powerful Space Explosion Ever Seen Reveals a Surprise Twist - ScienceAlert
mainText: In October 2022, the sky surveys monitoring for space explosions detected an unprecedented event. A source 2.4 billion light-years away emitted the largest burst of gamma radiation ever recorded. This event, known as GRB 221009A, reached a record 18 teraelectronvolts and was so powerful that it caused disturbances in Earth's outer atmosphere. The event, which was later nicknamed the BOAT (Brightest of All Time), was determined to be the birth of a black hole from the violent death of a massive star. A new analysis of the evolving light from this explosion has revealed some surprising details. Despite the immense gamma-ray fury of the BOAT, it was found to be surprisingly ordinary. "It's not any brighter than previous supernovae," says astrophysicist Peter Blanchard of Northwestern University in the US. "It looks fairly normal in the context of other supernovae associated with less energetic gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). You might expect that the same collapsing star producing a very energetic and bright GRB would also produce a very energetic and bright supernova. But it turns out that's not the case. We have this extremely luminous GRB, but a normal supernova." Gamma-ray bursts are the most powerful explosions observed in the cosmos. They are bursts of gamma radiation, the most energetic light in the Universe, that can erupt in 10 seconds with as much energy as the Sun will emit in 10 billion years. At least two major events are known to create a GRB: the formation of a black hole when a massive star goes supernova, or the hypernova accompanying the merger of two neutron stars. The types of novae that produce gamma-ray bursts are also thought to be responsible for the production of heavy elements in the Universe. Stars mostly form out of the hydrogen gas abundant in the Universe, but they smash together atomic nuclei in their cores to create heavier elements. This process tops out at iron, because the fusion of iron atoms consumes more energy than it generates. Elements heavier than iron can be formed in the violent throes of a giant cosmic explosion. And we've seen it! In the aftermaths of neutron star collisions, scientists have spotted elements too heavy to form via core fusion.

title: Starry Secrets: Scientists Uncover Hidden Role of the Milky Way in Ancient Egyptian Mythology - SciTechDaily
mainText: A recent study has unveiled the hidden role of the Milky Way in ancient Egyptian mythology. The study, conducted by an astrophysicist at the University of Portsmouth, reveals how the Milky Way might have accentuated the role of Nut, the Egyptian sky-goddess, and draws parallels between Egyptian beliefs and those of other cultures, underscoring the universal significance of celestial phenomena. Ancient Egyptians were known for their religious beliefs and astronomical knowledge of the Sun, Moon, and planets, but up until now it has been unclear what role the Milky Way played in Egyptian religion and culture. Nut is goddess of the sky, who is often depicted as a star-studded woman arched over her brother, the earth god Geb. She protects the earth from being flooded by the encroaching waters of the void, and plays a key role in the solar cycle, swallowing the Sun as it sets at dusk and giving birth to it once more as it rises at dawn. The paper draws on ancient Egyptian texts and simulations to argue that the Milky Way might have shone a spotlight, as it were, on Nut's role as the sky. It proposes that in winter, the Milky Way highlighted Nut's outstretched arms, while in summer, it traced her backbone across the heavens. The attached image shows the sky goddess Nut, covered in stars, is held aloft by her father, Shu, and is arched over Geb, her brother the Earth god. On the left, the rising sun (the falcon-headed god Re) sails up Nut’s legs. On the right, the setting sun sails down her arms towards the outstretched arms of Osiris, who will regenerate the sun in the netherworld during the night.

author: Universe Today
title: Radical NASA Study Says This Spacecraft Formation Could Reveal New Physics - ScienceAlert
mainText: A team of NASA researchers has recently proposed a novel approach to uncovering new physics within our Solar System. They suggest that spacecraft flying in a tetrahedral formation and using interferometers could aid this search. This mission could potentially solve a cosmological mystery that has puzzled scientists for over half a century. The proposal is the work of Slava G. Turyshev, a research scientist with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and adjunct professor of physics and astronomy at the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA). He was joined by Sheng-wey Chiow, an experimental physicist at NASA JPL, and Nan Yu, a senior research scientist at NASA JPL and adjunct professor at the University of South Carolina. Their research paper has been accepted for publication in Physical Review D. Turyshev's experience includes being a Gravity Recovery And Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) mission science team member. In previous work, Turyshev and his colleagues have investigated how a mission to the Sun's solar gravitational lens (SGL) could revolutionize astronomy. The concept paper was awarded a Phase III grant in 2020 by NASA's Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program. In a previous study, he and SETI astronomer Claudio Maccone also considered how advanced civilizations could use SGLs to transmit power from one solar system to the next. To summarize, gravitational lensing is a phenomenon where gravitational fields alter the curvature of spacetime in their vicinity. This effect was originally predicted by Einstein in 1916 and was used by Arthur Eddington in 1919 to confirm his General Relativity (GR). However, between the 1960s and 1990s, observations of the rotational curves of galaxies and the expansion of the Universe gave rise to new theories regarding the nature of gravity over larger cosmic scales.

author: Science X
title: Digging up new species of Australia and New Guinea's giant fossil kangaroos - Phys.org
mainText: Paleontologists from Flinders University have unearthed three unique new species of giant fossil kangaroos from Australia and New Guinea. These discoveries reveal that these extinct kangaroos were more diverse in shape, range, and hopping method than previously believed. The three new species belong to the extinct genus Protemnodon, which lived from around 5 million to 40,000 years ago. One of these species was about double the size of the largest red kangaroo living today. The research was prompted by the discovery of multiple complete fossil kangaroo skeletons from Lake Callabonna in arid South Australia in 2013, 2018, and 2019. These exceptional fossils allowed lead researcher Dr. Isaac Kerr, then a Ph.D. student, to solve a nearly 150-year-long puzzle about the identities of the species of Protemnodon. The new study from Flinders University reviewed all species of Protemnodon, finding that they were quite different from one another. The species adapted to live in differing environments and even hopped in different ways. Protemnodon would have looked something like a gray kangaroo, but were generally more squat and muscular. While some species were around 50 kg, others were much larger than any living kangaroo. However, one new species named as part of the latest study—named Protemnodon viator—was much bigger, weighing up to 170 kg. This is about twice as much as the largest male red kangaroos. Protemnodon viator was well-adapted to its arid central Australian habitat, living in similar areas to the red kangaroos of today. It was a long-limbed kangaroo that could hop fairly quickly and efficiently. Its name, viator, is Latin for "traveler" or "wayfarer."

title: IPL 2024, KKR vs RR Live Score: Jos Buttler leads Royals to record chase - Hindustan Times
mainText:
In a thrilling encounter during the Indian Premier League (IPL) 2024, the Rajasthan Royals (RR) achieved a remarkable victory against the Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR). The match took place at Eden Gardens in Kolkata on April 16, 2024.

KKR, batting first, posted an imposing total of 223 runs for the loss of 6 wickets in their allotted 20 overs. In response, the Rajasthan Royals displayed incredible resilience and determination. Led by Jos Buttler’s exceptional performance, RR successfully chased down the target with 0 balls remaining. Buttler’s magnificent century (107 runs off 60 balls) was the cornerstone of RR’s record-breaking chase. The Royals finished their innings at 224 runs for the loss of 8 wickets, securing a thrilling 2-wicket victory.

This high-scoring encounter showcased the best of T20 cricket, with both teams delivering outstanding performances. Jos Buttler’s heroics will be etched in IPL history as he led RR to an unforgettable win against KKR.

author: Daniel Nugent-Bowman
title: Connor McDavid's 100-assist season elevates already legendary career - The Athletic
mainText: Connor McDavid, the center for the Edmonton Oilers, has been making waves in the NHL scoring race. Despite a slow start to the season, McDavid has managed to catch up and even pull ahead of Nikita Kucherov of the Tampa Bay Lightning and Nathan MacKinnon of the Colorado Avalanche. With two goals and an assist in a 6-1 win against the Anaheim Ducks, McDavid has set up an exciting three-way dash to the Art Ross Trophy. McDavid has won the Art Ross as the League scoring champion five times in his first eight seasons. Despite a slow start with 10 points in his first 11 games this season, McDavid has been rapidly climbing the ladder. With 81 assists, McDavid is eight away from tying his career-high mark set last season. As it stands, McDavid is on pace to record over 100 assists, a feat no player has accomplished in the 21st century. The last player to reach the 100-assist mark was Wayne Gretzky, who recorded 121 with the Los Angeles Kings in 1990-91.

author: Lance Lysowski News Sports Reporter
title: Sabres fire head coach Don Granato in wake of another season out of the playoffs - Buffalo News
mainText: The Buffalo Sabres have announced the dismissal of head coach Don Granato, marking him as the seventh coach to be let go during the team's NHL-record 13-season playoff drought. The announcement came a day after the Sabres ended their season with a 4-2 victory over Tampa Bay. Despite finishing with a 39-27-6 record, the team had been ruled out of playoff contention the previous week. Granato, who had taken over on an interim basis during the COVID-19 pandemic-shortened 2021 season following the firing of Ralph Krueger, completed his third full season in Buffalo. The decision to let him go comes despite Granato having two seasons remaining on his contract, which included an extension set to begin next season. His record in Buffalo stands at 122-125-27. The team also announced the dismissal of assistant coach Jason Christie and video coordinator Matt Smith. The Sabres had a challenging season, managing to win three consecutive games only twice and frequently struggling to recover from slow starts. This was not the expectation for a team that had begun the season with GM Kevyn Adams declaring the window of contention open. The team's playoff drought is currently tied with the New York Jets for the longest active drought in North America's four major professional sports. This season, the Sabres were hampered by injuries to key players, inconsistent goaltending, a decision by the front office to add more youth to what was already the NHL's youngest roster, and a controversial change in coaching philosophy by Granato to shift the Sabres to a more defensive style. After finishing third in the NHL with 293 goals in the previous season, Buffalo's production fell to currently rank 22nd with 244 with two days left in the regular season. After finishing 26th in allowing 297 goals last season, the Sabres currently rank 11th in allowing 243. Poor starts were a significant factor in undermining Buffalo's season. The Sabres have allowed a league-worst 97 goals in the first period, while scoring just 67, which ranks 22nd.

author: Liz Roscher
title: Giannis Antetokounmpo to reportedly miss Bucks' early playoff games with calf strain, could return later - Yahoo Sports
mainText: Giannis Antetokounmpo, the two-time NBA MVP and star of the Milwaukee Bucks, is expected to miss the initial games of the playoffs due to a calf strain. The injury occurred during the Bucks' victory over the Boston Celtics on April 9. Antetokounmpo had an awkward landing on his leg, which was non-contact, and he was seen limping to the locker room. The Bucks immediately ruled him out of the game. Despite the non-contact nature of the injury, which often leads to severe concerns, it was a relief to hear that Antetokounmpo was only dealing with a calf strain. The Bucks announced on April 10 that Giannis would miss the team's final three regular-season games for rehabilitation, leaving his availability for the start of the playoffs uncertain. The Bucks, who are the third-seeded team in the Eastern Conference, are preparing for the playoffs without their star player. However, there is hope that Antetokounmpo could return at some point during the first round. The Bucks ended the season with a 1-2 record without Giannis. They will need to improve their performance as the playoffs begin. Their first-round series kicks off on Saturday with Game 1 against the sixth-seeded Indiana Pacers.

author: NCAA.org
title: Michigan committed NCAA violations in football program - NCAA.org
mainText: The University of Michigan and five individuals who are currently or previously associated with its football program have reached an agreement with the NCAA enforcement staff on recruiting violations and coaching activities by non-coaching staff members that took place within the football program. The penalties for these violations have also been agreed upon. A Committee on Infractions panel has approved this agreement. However, one former coach did not participate in the agreement, and that part of the case will be considered separately by the Committee on Infractions. The committee will release its full decision after this consideration. The agreed-upon violations involve impermissible in-person recruiting contacts during a COVID-19 dead period, impermissible tryouts, and the program exceeding the number of allowed countable coaches when non-coaching staff members engaged in on- and off-field coaching activities, including providing technical and tactical skills instruction to student-athletes. The negotiated resolution also involved the school's agreement that the underlying violations demonstrated a head coach responsibility violation and the former football head coach failed to meet his responsibility to cooperate with the investigation. The school also agreed that it failed to deter and detect the impermissible recruiting contacts and did not ensure that the football program adhered to rules for non-coaching staff members.

author: Steve Adams
title: Rangers To Promote Jack Leiter - MLB Trade Rumors
mainText: The Texas Rangers have announced that they will be promoting their top pitching prospect, Jack Leiter, to the major league roster. Leiter is set to make his big league debut on Thursday against the Detroit Tigers. The Rangers will need to make a corresponding move to accommodate Leiter, as they currently have a full 40-man roster. Leiter was drafted by the Rangers with the No. 2 overall pick in 2021. This promotion comes as an early birthday present for Leiter, who will turn 24 just three days after making his debut. Leiter comes from a family with a rich baseball history. His father, Al Leiter, is a two-time World Series champion and two-time All-Star. His uncle, Mark Leiter, had an 11-year career in the MLB, and his cousin, Mark Leiter Jr., is currently a setup man for the Chicago Cubs. Despite his impressive pedigree, Leiter's path to the majors has not been straightforward. He dominated in college at Vanderbilt, striking out 41% of his opponents in two seasons prior to being drafted. However, he struggled with command after being assigned to Double-A right out of the gate. Leiter walked more than 13% of his opponents and posted an ERA north of 5.00 in each of his first two seasons at the Double-A level. Despite these struggles, Leiter has been exceptional in his first three Triple-A appearances this season. In 14 1/3 innings, he has struck out 25 of his 57 opponents (43.9%), walked only three (5.3%), and surrendered just 11 hits. Four of those hits were home runs, which has resulted in a 3.77 ERA. However, his strikeout and walk trends are encouraging. The Rangers' rotation has been hit hard by injuries. Jacob deGrom and Max Scherzer, both of whom were acquired by the Rangers, opened the year on the 60-day injured list. Cody Bradford, a 26-year old southpaw, was also placed on the 15-day IL after a strong start to the season. Leiter will be joining a starting staff that includes Michael Lorenzen, Nathan Eovaldi, Jon Gray, and Dane Dunning.

title: Jayden Daniels, Drake Maye, JJ McCarthy, Michael Penix visiting Washington together - NBC Sports
mainText: The Washington Commanders are hosting a unique event today as they have invited all the quarterbacks they might draft to their facility at the same time. The list of invitees includes LSU quarterback Jayden Daniels, North Carolina quarterback Drake Maye, Michigan quarterback JJ McCarthy, and Washington quarterback Michael Penix. These four are among a large group of prospects who will all be in Washington this week as players make their final pre-draft visits. This is an unusual move for the Commanders to ask four different first-round quarterback prospects to come to the facility at the same time. With USC quarterback Caleb Williams a lock to go No. 1 to the Bears, Daniels has become a heavy favorite to go No. 2 overall to the Commanders. Maye and McCarthy are considered long shots, and Penix is an extreme long shot. Despite Daniels seeming to have the No. 2 spot all but locked up, Washington is acting like a team that remains undecided.

author: Mark Schlabach
title: Agent dismisses report of Rory McIlroy to LIV Golf for $850M - ESPN
mainText: Rory McIlroy, the four-time major championship winner, has denied a report that he had been offered $850 million and an equity stake in the LIV Golf League. McIlroy stated that he plans to finish his career on the PGA Tour. He also mentioned that neither he nor his agents have ever discussed a potential deal to lure him to the LIV Golf League, which is being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF). McIlroy expressed his surprise at how such rumors get started and reiterated his commitment to the PGA Tour. Sean O'Flaherty, McIlroy's agent, also confirmed that there was no truth to the report by City A.M., a London financial paper, about the second-ranked golfer in the world being offered such a deal.

author: John Stolnis
title: How does the DeVonta Smith contract affect A.J. Brown's future in Philadelphia? - Bleeding Green Nation
mainText: After being selected 10th overall in the 2021 NFL Draft, DeVonta Smith signed a four-year contract worth $20.141 million with the Philadelphia Eagles. The contract is fully guaranteed and contains a $12.008 million signing bonus. The four-year deal runs from 2021 to 2024 but has a fifth-year option that the Eagles can choose to exercise. DeVonta Smith’s impressive performance on the field has solidified his position as a key player for the Eagles, and his contract reflects the team’s confidence in his abilities. As for A.J. Brown, the impact of Smith’s contract remains to be seen. Brown, who is also a talented wide receiver, will likely negotiate his own contract in the future. The Eagles will need to carefully manage their salary cap to accommodate both players and maintain a competitive roster. The dynamic between Smith and Brown could shape the team’s receiving corps for years to come.

title: Celebrini tops Central Scouting North American ranking for 2024 NHL Draft - NHL.com
mainText: Macklin Celebrini, a center with Boston University in Hockey East, is No. 1 on NHL Central Scouting's final ranking of North American skaters for the 2024 Upper Deck NHL Draft. Central Scouting on Tuesday revealed its final list of the top North American skaters and goalies, and the top International skaters and goalies. Defenseman Anton Silayev of Torpedo in the Kontinental Hockey League is No. 1 on the final ranking of International skaters. Central Scouting held its final meetings with a five-day, in-person session in Toronto earlier this month following a two-day video conference to discuss and finalize the regional lists. The 2024 draft will reportedly be held at Sphere in Las Vegas, with the first round June 28 and Rounds 2-7 on June 29. The NHL Draft Lottery to determine the first 16 picks in the draft will be determined at a later date. "The top five players in the 2024 draft class are a very strong group, but there was no debate over who was No. 1," NHL Central Scouting director Dan Marr said. " [Celebrini is] an NHL All Star in the making, having been a model of elite consistency accumulating player and rookie of the year honors in Hockey East. "Macklin is playing at an enviable level all on his own. It's truly impressive how he is able to thrive in every environment he plays, possessing that rare ability with his skills and passion to face every challenge head-on and generate results all the while making himself a better player." Celebrini could become the second player from Boston University selected No. 1 in the NHL draft, joining goalie Rick DiPietro, who was chosen by the New York Islanders in 2000. He also could be the fourth player from NCAA men's college hockey chosen No. 1 and first since University of Michigan defenseman Owen Power by the Buffalo Sabres in 2021.

author: Liam Twomey
title: Breaking down Chelsea's farcical penalty squabble: 'You cannot behave like kids' - The Athletic
mainText: During Chelsea's 6-0 victory over Everton, a farcical penalty squabble took place that has drawn criticism from many quarters. The incident occurred when Chelsea were awarded a penalty after Cole Palmer, who scored four goals in the match, was fouled by Everton's Abdoulaye Doucoure. Noni Madueke and Nicolas Jackson, two of Chelsea's players, were seen arguing over who should take the penalty. This led to several other Chelsea players intervening in an attempt to defuse the situation. Ultimately, it was captain Conor Gallagher who took the penalty. Mauricio Pochettino, Chelsea's coach, expressed his displeasure at the incident, stating that such behavior is unacceptable. He emphasized that the players cannot behave like kids and must show more professionalism on the field.

author: Rob Rains
title: Former Cardinals manager Whitey Herzog dies at 92 - KSDK.com
mainText: Legendary St. Louis Cardinals manager Whitey Herzog has passed away at the age of 92. The news was confirmed by former KSDK Sports Director Jay Randolph. Known for his dynamic and fast-paced playing style, often referred to as "Whiteyball," Herzog led the Cardinals to a World Series championship in 1982. His successful tenure with the team continued into the late 1980s, with two more World Series appearances in 1985 and 1987. Herzog was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2010 and had a career total of 1,281 managerial wins with the Cardinals, Royals, Rangers, and Angels. The Cardinals announced Herzog's passing in a press release. The Herzog family issued a statement through the St. Louis Cardinals expressing their appreciation for the prayers and support they have received. They also noted that Whitey spent his last few days surrounded by his family and that his peaceful passing was a blessing for him. Herzog is survived by his wife of 71 years, Mary Lou Herzog, their three children; Debra, David and Jim, and their spouses; nine grandchildren and 10 great grandchildren. The Herzog family is planning a private celebration of life service after a period of grieving.

author: Mike Florio
title: Vikings need to pay Justin Jefferson or trade him to someone who will - NBC Sports
mainText: The Minnesota Vikings are facing a crucial decision regarding their star wide receiver, Justin Jefferson. The team needs to either pay him what he deserves or trade him to a team that is willing to do so. The situation has become increasingly urgent as Jefferson reportedly turned down a $30 million per year offer, indicating that he is seeking a higher value contract. The Vikings are clearly frustrated with the situation and are trying to portray themselves as reasonable in the negotiations. However, if they truly want to retain Jefferson, they need to meet his demands. If they are unable to do so, they should consider trading him to a team that can. The upcoming NFL draft could provide an opportunity for such a trade. There are speculations about potential trade scenarios, such as trading Jefferson and the 11th pick to the Commanders for the Jayden Daniels pick, or to the Patriots for the No. 3 pick. However, these are just speculations and the Vikings can put an end to these by simply paying Jefferson what he deserves. The longer the Vikings delay, the higher the price will become. This situation is not complicated, it's simply a matter of the Vikings deciding whether they are willing to pay Jefferson or not.

title: Watch: Furious Virat Kohli Kicks the Ground, Yells at RCB Teammates as SRH Unleash Mayhem - News18
mainText: During a boundary-laden clash between Royal Challengers Bengaluru and Sunrisers Hyderabad at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium, Virat Kohli was seen expressing his frustration.
