Winnipeg (0-3) has lost its first three games of the season for the first time since 2012. Backup Bombers quarterback Chris Streveler scored his third one-yard touchdown 2:10 into the fourth quarter to give Winnipeg the 21-20 lead. With 1:54 remaining, Adams marched the visitors down to Winnipeg's one-yard line and then took the knee to run out the clock. B.C. also got points off Whyte's field goals from 12, 14 yards and 31 yards. He made his pair of converts. Castillo was good on a 25-yard field goal and booted three converts. author: Summer Raemason
title: The hidden ‘capsule hotel’ plane areas you never knew existed onboard...
mainText: Secret 'capsule hotels' on planes are hidden resting areas for flight crew that many passengers are unaware of. These secure spaces provide a comfortable place for crew members to rest during long-haul flights, complete with mattresses, temperature controls, and ventilation. The areas vary in design from plane to plane and depend on the aircraft's age. Flight attendants have described the rest areas as cozy but potentially cramped for taller individuals. Crew members access these areas through hidden doors and ladders, often leading to beds where they can rest. Pilots have separate resting areas located above or near the cockpit, equipped with amenities like TVs and soundproofing. Despite the comfort provided, crew members must sometimes deal with disruptive passengers or challenging conditions while resting. These hidden spaces offer a glimpse into the behind-the-scenes operations of air travel, adding to the intrigue and mystery of flying. Flight attendants and private jet stewardesses have shared insights and secrets from their experiences, offering tips for travelers and revealing the unconventional requests they receive from passengers.

author: Gregory Wakeman
title: How to spend a weekend in Barcelona, with former F1 driver Jaime Alguersuari
mainText: Former F1 driver Jaime Alguersuari, now a DJ in Barcelona, shares his favorite spots in the city, from dining at Bar Cañete to enjoying the nightlife in Eixample. He highlights the unique geography of Barcelona, including Tibidabo Hill and La Barceloneta neighborhood, known for its beaches. Alguersuari recommends cultural experiences like visiting the National Museum of Art and exploring architecture by Antoni Gaudí. He suggests staying in the Sarrià neighborhood for a more relaxed atmosphere and enjoying Catalan cuisine at Bar Cañete. Outdoor enthusiasts can hike Tibidabo Hill for panoramic views and visit the Tibidabo Amusement Park. For nightlife, Alguersuari recommends Eixample area and bars like Dry Martini, along with clubs near the beaches. He also mentions events like the America's Cup and Brunch Electronik for music lovers. Barcelona's blend of culture, food, and atmosphere makes it a special place for Alguersuari, who appreciates its balanced energy and friendly people. His recommendations offer a local's insight into experiencing the vibrant city of Barcelona.

author: David Nikel
title: Why Norway Is Now A Year-Round Cruise Travel Destination
mainText: Norway's popularity as a cruise destination has been growing, with over six million passenger visits recorded in 2023. The traditional summer cruise season in the Norwegian fjords has expanded due to increased demand, with cruise lines extending their itineraries from as early as April to as late as September. Additionally, winter cruising in Norway is becoming more popular, especially for witnessing the northern lights during the solar maximum. Visitors can now explore Norway's fjords during different seasons, experiencing activities like the harvest season in autumn and enjoying winter sports like dog sledding and snow-shoeing. German cruise lines like AIDA Cruises and other European companies are also increasing their presence in Norway. Hurtigruten, a major player in Norwegian cruising, introduced new cruise routes, offering year-round options such as the 'Svalbard Line' and the 'North Cape Line'. With stricter environmental regulations for mainstream cruise ships, the expedition cruise market is growing, with the Arctic becoming a key destination. These expedition ships cater to activities like northern lights expeditions and whale-watching tours, even during the winter season. Norway's appeal as a cruise destination now extends beyond just the summer months.

author: Catherine Fry
title: Waikato dairy farmer Bruce Leonard’s lifetime of collecting and restoring tractors
mainText: ‘Retired’ dairy farmer Bruce Leonard is a big fan of Ford tractors. Catherine Fry finds out why. Bruce Leonard was raised on a dairy farm in Okoroire and is the first to say he didn’t like school at all, and left at 16 to go hay baling. He didn’t waste any time investing in his career and at 17 bought his first wheels, a hay baler, half on finance and half deposit. 'As a young man, I was working on our dairy farm too as it worked well with contracting, as they had opposite busy times.” Leonard became a fertiliser spreader driver in 1969. He went out on his own in 1989 and ran a fertiliser spreading business with his wife Gloria for 25 years from their 12-hectare home block. Leonard is now 'retired' and runs a 129-hectare dairy grazing block and raises beef on their home block. Leonard does find time for his tractor collecting and restoring. Always interested in Ford and Ferguson tractors, he bought his first one in 1989 from his family estate. The 4.4 litre, four-cylinder, 75hp diesel engine tractor was used for general agriculture work. It has 4WD, power steering and dual power shift transmission with 16 forward and four reverse gears. Leonard does encounter challenges with the tractors he collects and restores, such as a bearing problem in the gearbox of his Ford 6600 that required a significant repair job. Leonard is a member of the Rotorua Tractor and Machinery Club and enjoys showing his tractors off at their meet-ups in Mamaku and taking his Ferguson TEA on club treks. This article was originally published in Coast & Country News

author: Kem Ormond
title: Kem Ormond’s vegetable garden: Miner’s lettuce a must-have for winter salads
mainText: Kem Ormond is a features writer for NZME community newspapers and The Country. She’s also a keen gardener. OPINION What is a must-have staple for a winter salad, as it is around when there are not a lot of greens in your garden? Succulent, crisp, refreshing, delicious and so good for you - I am talking about miner’s lettuce (Claytonia perfoliata). Some people refer to it as Indian lettuce or winter purslane. It was what the miners used to eat over 150 years ago and is a historic American winter green, native to the West Coast of North America. We are so lucky it grows so well here in New Zealand. It likes cool, damp conditions to grow in and once happy in a spot - it is off! You can also grow some in pots or in an area where you can just let it seed under trees. Miner’s lettuce is also a reliable source of vitamins. I have read that just 100g of miner’s lettuce contain a third of your daily vitamin C, 10 per cent of iron, and 22 per cent of vitamin A. It also contains manganese, potassium, copper, and calcium. Seeds are rich in omega-3 fatty acids. So, you can cut down on buying supplements if you have this great plant in your garden. While you can buy seeds from local garden stores or seed suppliers, if you are a forager, you can also find this quite easily, especially at this time of the year. You need to be aware that the leaves do change shape over time. While they are bright green and heart-shaped when young, they tend to turn cup-shaped as the plant grows. At maturity, each rounded leaf will have clusters of small white flowers, or occasionally, slightly pink flowers. Once you know what to look for, you will start seeing it everywhere! As summer draws near, miner’s lettuce forms what looks like brown capsules which eventually burst, scattering its seeds. Leaving a few plants to seed will ensure it pops up again next year. While the leaves add a freshness to winter salads, you can also add young leaves into quiches, omelettes, soups, and sauces or add to sandwiches and fresh vegetable rolls. I harvest the leaves with a pair of scissors, and this seems to work well. I do not bother cooking the leaves as they are at their best when fresh and crisp. And if you find you get over-run with miner’s lettuce it is a great green crop to dig into the soil.

author: Megan Wilson
title: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: Hamilton mother fears daughter will develop AVCS
mainText: Teenager Jemima Thompson was given three years to live due to an abdominal condition – until she went to Germany and had a life-saving operation. Her younger sister Matilda died 11 years ago from what their mother Rachel Mckenna suspects was the same condition. Now, Mckenna fears for her youngest daughter, Clementine. A Hamilton mother who has lost one daughter and saved another from what she believes was the same rare and debilitating condition now fears her third daughter may develop it. Despite being raised in Rotorua, she says she may consider leaving New Zealand for a country with better care options if the public health system doesn’t change. Rachel Mckenna’s 5-year-old daughter Clementine was recently diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS). Clementine’s symptoms of the genetic connective tissue disorder are not life-threatening, but Mckenna fears they could be if she developed a co-morbidity, abdominal vascular compression syndromes (AVCS). Mckenna is knowledgeable about the two conditions after her eldest daughter, Jemima Thompson, was diagnosed and underwent surgery costing $160,000 in Germany last year. In 2013, Mckenna’s second eldest daughter, Matilda Thompson, died from what Mckenna suspects were the same conditions. A doctor in Germany told her the probability Matilda died from side effects from EDS due to AVCS was “evident” and he saw a predisposition in siblings with AVCS. Now, Mckenna fears for Clementine should she need treatment one day...

author: Rapid Recap Team
title: Editorial: What does the Matariki and the new year hold for Māori politics?
mainText: As Matariki approaches, the political landscape for Māori is filled with promise and contention. Te Pāti Māori is gaining significant support with its radical stance, advocating for a new parliament, declaration of independence, and revolution. The party demands a proportional share of the budget based on Māori demographics, pushing for significant systemic change. However, this confrontational approach may alienate some supporters looking for a less aggressive path. Māori voters now have a record 33 MPs across six parties, offering more choice. Senior figures like Winston Peters, David Seymour, Shane Reti, Marama Davidson, and others play key roles. Within this landscape, Labour struggles to provide coherent leadership while facing the challenge posed by Te Pāti Māori. Young MP Hana Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke has sparked youth interest in politics, but Te Pāti Māori's approach risks losing more conservative supporters to other parties. Key figures like National's Tama Potaka and Labour's Willie Jackson represent differing approaches, reflecting the diversity within Māori politics. Amidst a growing public discontent, Jackson's shift from union leader to politician and focus on the Treaty and Māori issues highlight his appeal. As Matariki prompts reflection and renewal, the future of Māori politics requires a balanced approach, integrating revolutionary ideas with pragmatic solutions to ensure meaningful progress while meeting Māori needs within a united national framework.
